maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: JURISDICTION OF RAILWAY COMMISSION IN CASES OF DAMAGES CAUSED BY ERECTION OF SNOW FENCES

speechtext:
Mr. 0. L. BOULANGER (Bellechasse) moved the second reading of Bill No. 5, to amend the Railway Act.
He said: I do not think it is necessary for me to say very much about this bill. It contemplates a minor amendment to the Railway Act, and it speaks for itself. It is hardly necessary to say that the bill is presented with the best of intentions. Its purpose is to afford some measure of relief to farmers who have difficulties with big railway corporations.
Section 203 of the general Railway Act gives the railway companies permission on or after the first day of November of each year to
Railway Act-Snow Fences

enter upon private lands alongside a railway and to erect snow fences on those private lands belonging to farmers. These snow fences cause the snow to accumulate on the land to a depth sometimes of twenty-five or thirty feet. I submit that this right which is given to the railway companies is absolutely out of the ordinary. It gives the companies power to enter upon property that does not belong to them. Of course, it is of great advantage to the railway companies, for it enables them to effect a great saving in labour and material. I do not think it is proper that the railways should have the right to make such a considerable saving at the expense of poor farmers.
It is true that at the present time section 203 of the act gives to the farmers the right to apply to the courts for redress; but eveiyone with experience in the practise of law knows that such a right involves a good deal of expense, much delay and a lot of trouble. The purpose of the bill is to provide a more expeditious, easy and economical way of settling these claims than by obliging the farmers to go to law. The damages sustained by the farmers are evident. These snow fences, especially those of more recent design, cause the snow to accumulate, as I have said, to a depth of twentj'-five or thirty feet, and that snow remains on the ground for a very long time in the spring.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: JURISDICTION OF RAILWAY COMMISSION IN CASES OF DAMAGES CAUSED BY ERECTION OF SNOW FENCES
speechtext: They must be removed on the first of April.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: JURISDICTION OF RAILWAY COMMISSION IN CASES OF DAMAGES CAUSED BY ERECTION OF SNOW FENCES
speechtext:
Yes, the snow fences are removed on the first of April, but the snow is not; the snow remains on the ground and only the sun can dispose of it. Take as an illustration my own parish of St. Charles de Bellechasse where I was born and brought up. That parish was settled about the middle of the eighteenth century. In fact it was established in 1745. The railway through that parish was built in 1855, and it is no fault of the farmers if their farm buildings, their orchards and their gardens are in proximity to the line. Their farms, their gardens and their orchards were there before the railway was built. The railway was built through the most settled part of the country, through farms, adjacent to buildings and houses, through vegetable and strawberry patches, gardens, orchards and so on. What happens is this. In the fall the railway people enter upon these farms without permission and erect snow fences. True, on the first of April these fences are removed but the snow remains for quite a long time. Sometimes it is there until June. It leaves the land entirely unsuitable for vegetable and fruit growing especially, and also causes fruit trees

to freeze and die. It is responsible for considerable damage, and the only recourse of the farmers is to go to law, running the risk of having their cases dragged from the court of first instance to the court of appeal, and incurring a lot of costs.
I propose to do away with this system and have the board of railway commissioners decide upon these eases. As everyone knows, the board of railway commissioners is not bound by any strict rules of procedure. It settles cases in an equitable and amicable way, and it is not obliged to observe the rules of procedure that are followed in courts of law. That is one advantage; but the major advantage is, of course, that before the board of railway commissioners there are no costs. It is a poor man's court, because there is no tariff of fees applicable to cases heard before the board. This would be a great advantage to the farmers. Another advantage would be that the board of railway commissioners could settle these cases once for all. The board could have their engineers or their officials look into the situation on any farm and come to a fair conclusion as to what the damages might be from year to year, and with that estimate before them could make a definite settlement once for all of such claims. A settlement of this kind cannot be made in the ordinary courts because those courts can only assess damages that have already occurred; they cannot give anything for damages which a plaintiff has not yet suffered. Moreover, they are obliged to adjudicate upon cases where the damages have occurred within two years of the date of submission of the claim to the courts. According to the law of the province of Quebec-and I believe it is pretty much the same in the other provinces-claims for damages of this description are outlawed after two years, and so the farmers in our section have to take action every two years for settlement. The board of railway commissioners is not bound by the civil code of the province of Quebec or by the rules of procedure of that province, and under the Railway Act it could be provided that the board shall settle all these claims once for all-with regard not only to damages that have already been sustained but also to any damages which farmers are likely to suffer in the future.
Last year when the bill was presented to the house the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) had a few objections to make. One was that the board did not wish to take on any more work. That is only natural. They think that they already have enough to do. I do not believe, however, that this bill would result in any great increase in the work they

Railway Act-Snow Fences
have to do. Their duties would be increased only to an infinitesimal extent, and I am sure that if they look at the matter again they will decide that their objection is not a very serious one. They might have one case or two or three or four cases a year in a section of the country where there was a great accumulation of snow, but that is not the condition in all parts of Canada. Another of their objections, as the minister told us last year, was that the litigants would have to come to Ottawa to plead their cases. In practice this is no objection, because in practice litigants do not travel to appear before the board of railway commissioners; the members of the board travel to meet the litigants. They go about the country, to Regina, Winnipeg, Vancouver, Montreal, Quebec, Rimouski, Halifax, as the case may be, and meet the litigants where the litigation arises and the witnesses are available and the record exists. Therefore the objection does not seem very serious; there would be no change in the procedure of the board because it is travelling already. The only difference would be that instead of having five or six cases at a session in Winnipeg, for example, they might have seven or eight.
Another objection which was raised by the minister last year was that there now is a system of arbitration provided for the settlement of these cases. Under that system the complainant and the railway company each appoint an arbitrator, and a third arbitrator is appointed by a judge. In regard to this arbitration system I think the minister has been misinformed. It applies in the case of lands required for the construction of railways, but, if I read the law correctly, it does not apply to damages caused by the operation of a railway. When damage is caused by railway operation complainants have to go before the ordinary courts; it is like any other action for damages. You have to take action in the ordinary way, follow the procedure, and run all the risks of cases in courts.
This risk of costs results in great injury to the farmer, because it is exploited to the limit by the railway claims agents. I do not blame them for that; it is their job to discourage claims against the railways, and they use all the arguments that they can invoke. They go to the farmer who has a claim against the railway company on the ground that his land was covered by thirty feet of snow, thus preventing the planting of potatoes or strawberries in time, or whose fruit trees have been damaged or killed by frost during the winter on account of accumulation of snow, and they say: We will fight you in the courts; your farm will be
eaten up in costs if you do not accept the offer we are making. And of course the poor farmer gets scared and accepts in settlement of his claim an amount which is perhaps a mere fraction of the real damage he has suffered.
If these claims could come before a tribunal where there is no risk of costs it would be a great service to the farmers. I am sure the board of railway commissioners is competent to adjudicate on these small damage actions. I do not know all the members of the board but I know a few of them; for instance I know well the chairman and the vice-chairman. They are capable lawyers of great experience; they have been in public life, and they possess the milk of human kindness. I am confident that they would be able to deal with these cases admirably, and would deal with them in the interest of and to the advantage of the farmers.
I will not say more, sir, because the bill speaks for itself. The arguments in favour of it are self-evident, and I commend it to the consideration of the house.

maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: JURISDICTION OF RAILWAY COMMISSION IN CASES OF DAMAGES CAUSED BY ERECTION OF SNOW FENCES
speechtext:
I rise to say a word in support of this bill. I am pleased that the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Boulanger) has brought the matter before the house. It is a great inconvenience and cause of loss to farmers to have these snow fences erected on their farms. But the railway companies are not the greatest sinners in that regard; provincial, county and in some cases municipal highways are protected in the same way. The railways and the provincial and municipal authorities, without asking the farmer's consent, go on his property and erect snow fences, probably twenty-five yards inside the road fence. These snow fences catch a very large amount of snow during the winter. I have seen field after field where by reason of the accumulation of snow it was ten days to two weeks after the rest of the field was sown before the farmer could cultivate that land along the road. Also I have seen the crop there damaged, because a late crop is never as good as one sown earlier.
It has always seemed to me a great injustice that public bodies can go on a farmer's land in this way. I speak from personal experience. In some cases the fences are not removed by April 1. The inconvenience to the farmer is considerable and something should be done. I am heartily in accord with the provisions of the bill.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Transport) :
maintopic: RAILWAY ACT AMENDMENT
subtopic: JURISDICTION OF RAILWAY COMMISSION IN CASES OF DAMAGES CAUSED BY ERECTION OF SNOW FENCES
speechtext:
This bill makes a substantial change in the method of dealing with cases affecting
534	COMMONS
Government Railways Act-Snow Fences
snow fences adjacent to railways. It cancels the present method of dealing with such cases, and provides a new one. Perhaps in order to refresh our memories I might read the relevant section of the Railway Act:
203. Every railway company may, on and after the first day of November, in each year, enter into and upon any lands of His Majesty or of any person lying around the route or line of the railway, and erect and maintain snow fences thereon, subject to the payment of such land damages, if any actually suffered, as are thereafter established, in the manner provided by law with respect to such railways.
By this bill the words "in the manner provided by law" are to be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
. . . by mutual agreement, and failing such agreement, by the board of railway commissioners for Canada, who shall determine and fix the compensation to be paid the owner by way of damages. Such compensation shall be determined and fixed by the board, where possible, in respect to future as well as present or past damages suffered by the said owner.
I think my hon. friend misunderstood my objection of last year, when he said it was that the board of railway commissioners would be overworked. I admit at once that the board of railway commissioners is one branch of the government that is not overworked at the present time, and I have no objection to this bill on that score. I do believe, however, and it is the opinion of my own officers and of the railway board, that the present method of disposing of these claims is less cumbersome, more expeditious and apt to be more just than the method now suggested in substitution therefor.
The present procedure is very simple. The railway and the person damaged attempt to reach an agreement. If they fail they go to the local judge, who practically acts as arbitrator between the two parties. If either party is dissatisfied with the decision of the local judge that decision can be appealed to the higher court in the province, but unless the amount in question is in excess of $5,000 the appeal is limited to one higher court. In that way it becomes a local matter. The hen. gentleman who made this motion said that the question involves the height of the snowdrifts, the damage to trees and a number of other considerations in connection with which local knowledge is of immense importance in arriving at a decision. Usually the parties to the dispute, including the judge, are residents of the locality. They understand these matters and are able to arbitrate the case in a satisfactory manner.
As I say, this bill sets aside that procedure. No longer will it be possible to place the matter before the local judge. It now becomes mandatory that the case be brought before

the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada. I will admit at once that it is a debatable point whether this is a better procedure than the other, but I might point out that the railway commission would be strangers to the locality in question. It is true that once a year, or perhaps once in two years, the board travels from coast to coast holding sittings at various centres, but even hearings of that kind will not make the board familiar with the particular facts in disputes of this kind. I question very much whether the decision of the board would be more just or more acceptable to both parties than the decision rendered under the present procedure.
There is, of course, another matter involved. This bill would change the functions of the board of railway commissioners. In 1916, 1917 and 1918 a great deal of pressure was brought to bear on parliament to place the jurisdiction over the settlement of land disputes as between the railways and the public in the hands of the board of railway commissioners. At that time the board very strongly took the stand that they were not constituted for that purpose; that their machinery was not suitable for that purpose, and that decisions of that kind should be left to the ordinary courts. The board take exactly the same position in this case; that is, that their machinery is not suitable for deciding cases of this kind. However, I think the fundamental question is whether the citizens of Canada would be better served by the new type of court proposed by the bill or by the present procedure, and I believe that matter should be studied by a standing committee of this house. I therefore suggest, Mr. Speaker, that this bill be read a second time and referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

He said:	Mr. Speaker, this second bill
amends the Government Railways Act, and it is introduced for this reason: The Government Railways Act is still on the statute books, and there is a question as to whether or not it is still applicable to the railways which were formerly government property and which now form part of the Canadian

Criminal Code-Motor Cars
National Railways. That question has not been decided in a definite and categorical manner, and the act contains a provision in regard to damages caused by snow fences. Therefore, in order to be on the safe side, I am also presenting this bill to amend the Government Railways Act.
I am not going to repeat what I said when I explained the bill which has just been given second reading, beyond this: A moment ago the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) said that the procedure before the board of railway commissioners would be different from the procedure which exists at the present time before the superior courts, for instance. I do not see that there would be any difference. If the bill passed we would proceed before the board of railway commissioners exactly as we now proceed before the superior court. The plaintiff would bring his evidence; he would produce his witnesses and would present his written proof before the board just as he does before the superior court at the present time. The only difference would be this: At the present time if he loses his case before the superior court he may have to pay hundreds of dollars in costs to lawyers on both sides. Under the new system proposed, if the plaintiff lost his case before the board of railway commissioners he would not have to pay a cent in costs.
The minister says, "Well, the members of that board are not familiar with that kind of work. They are not as well able to adjudicate in these small damage actions as the local judge would be." I know that Mr. Garceau, for instance, the vice-chairman of the board, is an experienced lawyer in Quebec, and I am sure that Mr. Garceau, with his knowledge of the civil law of that province and with his long experience, could decide a small damage action just as well as any judge of the superior court or the circuit court. I would not be afraid to go before Mr. Garceau, where I am sure I would obtain a decision just as equitable as I might obtain from the judge of any court. The board goes to Quebec, for instance, many times a year. The litigants of that district would go to the courthouse, where they go now. They cannot go anywhere else. If they have a damage action against the railways they have to go to the court-house now to have it adjudicated upon, so in that respect the procedure would be just the same, but instead of going before Mr. Justice So-and-So of the superior court they would go before the board of railway commissioners, in the same building. They would proceed exactly in the same way. They
would make out their case in the same way, and receive a decision just as good as they could receive from a court. The only difference would be that they would not have to pay hundreds of dollars in costs, if they lost their cases.

speechtext:
Mr. T. L. CHURCH (Broadview) moved the second reading of Bill No. 10, to amend the criminal code.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, in moving the
second reading of the bill, I wish to call the attention of the house to the great slaughter occurring on our highways. Almost every road is coloured red with the slaughter of men, women and children. This slaughtering is done in a manner that is disgraceful, and presents the most important domestic problem with which we have to deal this year. I may say that it is one of Canada's chief problems, and parliament does nothing about it.
We are satisfied to devote a whole lot of time to flag waving, but the government of the day does not seem prepared to sit down and consider what must be done for these helpless men, women and children whose homes have been ruined and whose lives have been wrecked. All this goes on, and yet this high court of parliament sits here and does nothing to deal with these practical problems, which would be a work for the benefit of the people. They do nothing but appoint commissions, and that kind of thing.
I believe a few facts should be drawn to the attention of the house. The subject of the bill has been discussed in the house for three or four sessions. One of the commandments of God is: Thou shalt do no murder. Many men of real worth, through carelessness and selfishness, are recklessly violating not only the laws of God but those of men. No invention has contributed more to the comforts of our people than has the motor car, but, like every other invention we must consider its use as one thing and its abuse as another.
Criminal Code-Motor Cars

During the past century scientific discoveries in medicine, chemistry and physics have resulted in untold good to humanity, but, as in the abuse of inventions, in war they were a curse to mankind. In like manner, to-day the abuse of the motor car is a curse to mankind. Looking into the question one finds invariably a tremendous annual loss from deaths, accidents, injuries, and so on. One finds untold sorrow and suffering with intense pain and grief, almost exceeding anything the human imagination could conceive. The suffering brought about by these machines is equalled only by that inflicted by plagues, pestilence, famine, battle, murder and sudden death.
It would be misleading and unfair to attempt to attribute all the blame for these horrors on the highways to all people who drive and use motor cars. The fact is that ninety-five per cent of drivers are trying to obey the law. It is the remaining five per cent about whom I am complaining. They cause the trouble. One has only to see the records to understand the facts. As I study the records of cases I am driven to the conclusion that beyond any doubt the small minority are the major cause of the trouble. They appear to have exploited, for their own pleasure and profit, the generous tolerance of others. They use their cars in an irresponsible, careless and unchristian way. The fault is grievous, and they can have no ground for complaint if they are put under restraint through application of the criminal code. Ignorance and thoughtlessness are not palliatives. Obedience is the only reparation they can make, and it is long overdue.
I should like to quote the observations of the late Chief Justice R. M. Meredith, who was on the supreme court bench for about forty years. These are his words:
And as now nearly everyone is a car owner, and car driver, young and old, of all sorts and conditions, it is difficult to get justice in even a civil action. Car-driver jurors have nearly all the speed fever; and self-preservation instincts are so strong that they will not be persuaded to decide against drivers who have been no more unlawful than they themselves often, if not commonly, are.
What then is the remedy? I think it should be; make the laws plain and reasonably severe and enforce them; and cancel licences freely. And at the other end of the matter, give no licence to anyone who is not proved to be mentally and physically, and from experience and a knowledge of the highway laws, thoroughly capable.
As I see it, the situation calls for united effort on the part of church members, community clubs, boards of trade, municipal councils and, in fact, all public bodies. Great sorrows, broken lives and shattered homes

resulting from such holocaust are just as real as the nation's supreme sorrow following the war. How long will this suffering have to continue?
I believe three features dominate the conduct of motor traffic to-day. First, we must consider the indifference shown by the five per cent of drivers of the rights and privileges of the people using the highways. Then, there is the indifference to the convenience of others; there is excessive speed, and congestion. Ever since man has learned to direct a machine more powerful than himself he has asserted his superiority over his neighbour. "Make way or take the consequences" is the cry of the reckless driver. Yet, this indifference is limited to only a small number. Fortunately only a small group out of the large body of drivers is responsible for the damage. The majority of motor car drivers have only a hazy knowledge of the mechanism of their machines. For absolute control, the only condition in which a car is fit to be driven at thirty miles an hour is when there is perfect adjustment and perfect conditioning. Even so the machine is potentially as dangerous as a loaded gun, and must be handled with equal care and vigilance. A moment's inattention may be fraught with dire results. Every motor vehicle is a dangerous implement, even when controlled by the most expert, and requires incessant vigilance in all circumstances, and especially at speeds above thirty miles an hour.
As I said, transportation should be a means to an end, not an end in itself. I say when the matter is brought before the house and the Department of Justice it is not treated as it should be. It is a major problem, and it is almost impossible for administrators and legislators to give too much time to it. Inside of an hour after the adjournment of a debate is moved, more people are killed. If wooden crosses were used to represent the people who in twelve months have been killed or injured by motor cars they would, if placed a foot apart, cover parliament hill and reach to Lansdowne park. The figures show that last year in the city of Toronto sixty-eight people were killed, 3,608 hurt and 170 drivers were gaoled. In 1938, to date, there are six dead, 295 hurt and 36 drivers gaoled.
I have received the totals from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics; I do not know whether or not it is permissible to place two or three small tables on Hansard, but I believe if I may be permitted to do so it will assist hon. members in realizing the gravity of the problem. One table, No. 13, gives the number of deaths resulting from automobile accidents between the years 1927 and 1936.

In France, with a population of 42,000,000, 4,415 people were killed in motor accidents in 1936; in Germany, where they are spending vast sums on road building, with a population of 67,000,000, the number of people killed last year was S,381; in the United States, with a population of 128,000,000, in motor accidents in 1935, 37,000 people were killed, or half the number of their soldiers who were killed in the great war; in England an average of twenty people are killed each day, or about 6,000 in a year. The figures for England last year were 6,000 killed and 200,000 injured in motor accidents. I am taking these figures from the House of Lords report.
In England, in the ten years up to December of last year, 66,000 were killed and 2,000,000 injured in motor accidents. Fancy, in the mother country alone, 66,000 people being killed and 2,000,000 injured on the highways! An average of two children are killed per day in England. In one year in England 50,000 school children were killed or injured. These accidents are estimated to cost the nation £200,000,000 a year. This estimate is from a new textbook on public highways, published in London, which I am sorry is not available in the library here. It is frequently referred to by the Minister of Transport in England, and I hope the Parliamentary Library will get a copy. That is to say, in a year there are more people killed than there were soldiers killed in the whole Boer war. The hospitals in England are all facing deficits from road accidents. The cost of English hospitals is estimated at three hundred thousand pounds a year.
I ask the government very seriously to consider this question and to let parliament know what they intend to do about it. The traffic on the English roads is very great, greater than elsewhere. In the United States, for example, there are eight cars to every mile; in France, four cars to every mile; Germany, fifteen; England, ten; and in Canada, fifteen. In Canada to-day deaths as a result of motor accidents are a great national scandal.
The key to the situation, in my opinion, is the human factor. The wider the roads, the more numerous the accidents. An examination of one hundred thousand cases of road accidents in the mother country over a period of two and a half years has been kindly sent to me, with a very fine letter of information, by the present Secretary of War, the Right Hon. Hore-Belisha, who so ably presided over the transport department in England for three or four years. I have not

time to read it, and I wish I could be allowed to put it on Hansard. I can give a few figures to show what that great Minister of Transport did in the old land, where they have some of the best roads in the world. When they reduced the speed limit to thirty miles an hour the accidents dropped by fifty per cent, and if they could get the speed down to twenty miles per hour the number of accidents would decrease at a further rate. I should like the minister to see a copy of this report which Mr. Hore-Belisha has sent to me; it is a very valuable and interesting document. Mr. Hore-Belisha finds that the relative severity of accidents in areas not built up, and1 where speeds would normally be higher, is greater; that the proportion of accidents which occur at junctions, especially in built-up areas, is very high; that over one-third of the persons injured were pedal cyclists; over twenty-nine per cent, pedestrians, and over eighteen per cent, motor cyclists or their passengers.
He goes on to refer to the comparative severity of casualties to motor cyclists, over one-third being either killed or seriously injured, and the report gives tables in which the accidents are classified.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the key to the whole problem is the human factor, and a study of these cases shows that the wider the roads, and the more you spend on them the more accidents there will be. These accidents, it is shown, occur in clear, not foggy, weather, and it is on week-ends and at Christmas and other holidays that most of the accidents occur. In Canada the bulk of accidents occur after April and continue to the end of the year, especially the summer weekends and Christmas.
I doubt if our roads policy in this country is a wise one. We have our good roads associations and they are urging legislatures to build more roads; our uneconomic roads creating railway deficits are a nuisance, and I think we have the most uneconomic road system in the world. They compete against our railways, on which we have spent four billion dollars. We allow motor trucks and buses on roads to be used on roads built fifty years ago for horse-drawn traffic, and we let modern motor cars drive over these same roads at a very fast pace of from fifty to sixty miles an hour. It was the railways that ruined the canals a hundred years ago, and today it is the motor buses and motor cars that are ruining the railways. The mortality in these road accidents is appalling. Canada's rate is high; England's rate is not as high

Criminal Code-Motor Cars
as that of the United States or Germany, but it is higher than that of France and Canada for our population. It is a living scandal of first importance; it is disgraceful.
Another menace on our congested highways is the glaring headlights, which in conjunction with beer parlours and the truck traffic, make it impossible to drive in safety in Ontario at night, and conditions are getting worse. Lord Justice Maughan, that great jurist who so ably sat in the privy council said in the House of Lords last fall that all "his experience on the bench went to show that a stiffening of the law would tend most substantially to reduce the number of accidents on the roads." The new wider roads in Germany have not reduced accidents, and in England the experience is that there is an increased mortality in road accidents resulting from the straightening and widening of roads permitting of higher speeds. We as a House of Commons know we can reduce these accidents and we meet and do nothing about it, nor do the press or church.
Compare the accidents in the air or on the railways with motor car accidents and you will find that they are almost negligible in comparison with the holocaust on the highways of this country. At level crossings we have our bells and wig-wags, but according to a return brought down in this house last year there were 175 accidents at level crossings, in which 84 people were killed and 208 injured. The problem is so pressing that there should be no more delay. The government's policy is not simply laissez-faire; it is laissezmaourir- let the people die as they like-let them die for all the government cares. I say, Mr. Speaker, it is impossible to allow such conditions to continue longer in this country. The present slaughter cannot be allowed to continue. Accidents largely arise through a lack of courtesy or because of impatience, hurry, bad manners or because one driver forgets his duty to his God and neighbour and refuses to give way to another.
What is the church of God doing while all this is going on? When we had an epidemic of infantile paralysis all over this country, caused by ragweed and other conditions, the deaths from which were trivial in number compared with the number killed in motor car accidents, the whole press of this country was aroused. We all remember that terrible college disaster at St. Hyacinthe, which is a reflection on our building laws and fire prevention regulations. There was mourning all over Canada for the people of our fine province of Quebec and sympathy with the grief of the parents of the young children who perished in
that terrible disaster, and with the heads of that fine seminary of learning and education. If any disease were to take the toll of the motor car, medicine and science would know no rest until some cure for the disease had been found. Look at the figjit that science and preventive medicine are making against cancer, tuberculosis, diabetes and other ills. But hundreds of thousands, Mr. Speaker, are being slaughtered or severely injured in motor car accidents in this country; yet the press and the church say little or nothing about it and give little attention to it. We need to deal with this problem along bolder lines.
I want constructive action from the government. True, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) is overworked and has already a heavy department and I doubt if we should put this work on him. I was not in the house the other day when a just tribute was being paid to him, but I have known him for a great many years and I am sure he sympathizes very deeply with the object I have in view in this bill and would do all he could to prevent the slaughter, if he could go further, as he always strives to do good. We want definite and immediate action. Constitution or no constitution, something must be done without further delay to prevent this slaughter. Our road system fails to provide the safety it should for pedestrians and cyclists and farmers. In the South African war, lasting two and three-quarter years, there were 7,492 people killed. During a period of the same length in England 16,000 people were killed in motor car accidents. People nowadays in their mad rush and hurry hold life less sacred than they used to, but the grief of parents mourning for their children, the grief of husbands and wives, is just as deep as that of those who lost members of their families in the South African war.
What is the government going to do about it n'ow? These casualties are the more deplorable in that too often they mean that wives and young children are left without the breadwinner. During the South African war it was usual for Queen Victoria to receive news of its progress and of the casualties. One day the war minister walked in and told her that twenty-three of her soldiers had been killed the previous day. The poor old queen wept, and said, "Let a telegram be sent to the relatives of every one of these men." If the king in these days were to send a telegram to the relatives of the 6,000 people who were killed and the 200,000 who were injured as a result of motor accidents in England last year, he would have no time to do anything else.
Criminal Code-Motor Cars

It shows that to-day we hold life less sacred than we used to do. In my opinion the church of God should be up and doing. It is not doing all it should do; it should take some constructive action. Are our Canadian people entirely lacking in any sense of balance while all this goes on?
I have already referred to the dangers of delay. The pedestrian, in crossing the street, is somewhat to blame. There has been some reduction in the number of child casualties because the cities have guides to conduct children across the streets.
In my opinion this is a great national evil, and it is a shocking and scandalous state of affairs that it is going on all over the country without anything being done by anybody. What do the legislatures of this country do? Nothing. What does this high court of parliament at Ottawa do? One of its branches, the senate, goes off on a three weeks' holiday, saying, "We have no work." There is work to do right here. Look at what the House of Lords did in regard to this question. Would our senate do it? No chance! I have before me the report of a debate in the House of Lords, in which right honourable and right reverend prelates of the church of England who took part emphasized the importance of dealing with an evil which is crippling the mother country by depriving her of the flower of the nation, the youth of the day. I ask the church of Canada to be up and doing, to bring this problem to the attention of the people and of parliament. It is not a political question-far from it. I put it before the minister at this time and hope to be able to offer some constructive suggestions. The Right Honourable and Right Reverend Bishop of Winchester in the House of Lords made some splendid practical suggestions. This right reverend prelate called the country to arms to stop it all.
Coming to the bill itself, on the second reading we can discuss only the principle of the measure not the clauses. As regards the clause referring to drunken drivers, the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) made in the last debate a very wise remark about beer parlours, which was taken up by a section of the press, about drunken drivers, and the experience of other countries confirms what the hon. member said. My right hon. leader also alluded to this matter in a very able address he made last session. I have drafted a new clause this year to take care of this point, because, according to some judges, you cannot convict or it is hard to convict under the present section of the

criminal code which is full of loopholes. I have therefore stricken out the old clause and substituted:
(4) Every one who, while under the influence of alcohol or of any narcotic, to such a degree as to make him incapable of exercising a safe and proper control of any motor vehicle or automobile, drives or attempts to drive such motor vehicle or automobile, is guilty of an offence-
And why should he not be? Why are these people allowed to go out in such a condition on highways built for traffic as it was fifty years ago, roads constructed in the ox-cart days, as were our rural and some suburban and urban roads-for I do not refer altogether to the improved roads. Why are they allowed to go out on roads suitable only for horses and horse-drawn vehicles and rush recklessly along at fifty to sixty miles an hour, to send people into the cemetery in the twinkling of an eye? I say it is all wrong. It is race suicide.
We then come to another section, "Racing and cutting in." The investigation made by the Minister of Transport in England shows what terrible tragedies result from this practice. The right honourable prelate in the House of Lords, the Bishop of Winchester, called this pest "cads."
On page 2 also is a subsection, "Causing death in a culpably negligent manner." It takes two people to make an accident, and the question of fact is for the jury. In many cases the decision has been taken from the jury.
"Person having caused death not to drive for two years." Why should a man who has killed another person be allowed to drive within two years? In my opinion he should not drive any more. I know that if I killed a person I would not want to drive again.
It is also provided that persons shall not drive if under eighteen years of age. Objection may be taken to that clause. May I inform the house that, in the debate in the House of Lords, speaker after speaker rose and said that nobody can drive a locomotive on a private right of way unless he is a skilled man, and yet immature boys and girls of fourteen and sixteen are permitted to drive cars. I was on the street the day before Christmas. A Toronto Transportation Company street car was diverted down Bay street along Wellington between Bay and Yonge to get around the loop more quickly. There were trucks about, and one truck blocked the street car. The motorman and the conductor got out to move the truck. There were about twenty-five passengers in the

Criminal Code-Motor Cars
street car. But neither conductor nor motor-man could move the truck. A boy of twelve moved the truck. He was asked how old he was and he said he was twelve years of age. He could drive when he is twelve; boys who say they are fourteen think they should be entitled to drive when they are only eleven. Remember the accident at Vineland last September, where a school boy who was driving four or five of his companions, girls and boys, towards a railway crossing did not hear the bell or see the train, and all of them were blotted out. I agree with the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Thompson) that the age limit should be raised. The motor car is the most dangerous mechanism that we have. Why should somebody of immature age and judgment be allowed to drive? The Reverend Mr. Austin Ireland, M.A., anglican rector of Thorold, who conducted the burial service on these Vineland people, cried out from the pulpit to parliament to put a stop to such conditions, and driving by children of immature age although some are good drivers. No doubt many of our best drivers are quite young, but owing to the abuse of the permission to people to drive when under age, something should be done about it.
As to confiscating cars, if one looks over the criminal code he can find many confiscatory clauses. They confiscate pistols; they confiscate all kinds of things of personal property under the code; why should not parliament extend the power to cover such criminal offences by drivers of cars?
To cover all the matters referred to would take too long, for there are other bills to be considered.
Regarding driving when a licence has been suspended, that has been done in many cases, and it is only common sense that under the code this should be made an offence and a penalty exacted. Also we have those hit and run drivers, the cowardly people who leave their victims lying on the pavement. I could show hon. members some photographs of these victims-.men and women and little children, even babies, knocked down on the road, and the drivers have escaped. The section should be stiffened up all along the line.
I have mentioned that the court may impound the motor car. Why should not a person who drives recklessly or negligibly a highly dangerous machine not have the control of it taken away from him? Why should not the licence of such a person be revoked? No wonder people are being killed; our criminal code is twenty years behind the times in the way it deals with this problem. It is the function of juries to take the law
to be what the judge says it is, but to decide questions of fact, but in a large number of cases the judge takes the case away from the jury and allows the defendant to go free.
This bill is not perfect by any means. I do not profess that it is. I cannot be expected, as a private member without adequate help, to do all -that is required. I have brought the problem forward a number of times and laid it before this parliament. I have done my duty as I see it. I have no apologies to make. What are hon. members going to do about it? Are they going to allow the respected Minister of Justice just to rise after I sit down and move the adjournment of the debate, or are they going to continue this discussion and demand immediate action? A great prelate said in the House of Lords that this was the most important domestic problem England had. The Bishop of Winchester, who made that remark, also told the House of Lords that if they did nothing else but continue to sit every day for a month until they solved the problem, their time would be well spent, and this was the solemn duty of administrators and legislators. The representative of the Minister of Transport in the House of Lords was asked what he intended to do about it. He was not allowed to escape by moving the adjournment of the debate, but had to appoint a select committee. He offered to appoint a commission, but the House of Lords, being practical men, would not accept that suggestion. The matter had been made a football of long enough. They wanted a committee. After what I have seen of committees, however, I have not, for some of these select committees, the respect I used to have.
I submit that the road contractors and cement people have too much influence in these good conventions at the present time. They go up and down the country, they go to the conventions, and they have such influence both in and outside the conventions that they will do anything to persuade the legislature to spend more money on existing uneconomic roads. Let the government announce some practical action here and now.
I have given only a small portion of the facts I have, and if the minister has no objection I should like to put on the record the two pages of tables from which I quoted. In fact, I read most of it. It was obtained from the bureau of statistics and it would give hon. members a good idea of the situation.
That is all I have to say in moving the second reading of this bill. I make the motion m the hope that something will be done, and I trust that other members will speak. They have an opportunity to-day to
Criminal Code-Motor Cars

take part in the debate now or never. They know the findings of their magistrates and county court judges and juries all over Canada. Let us support the law officers of the crown; let us support law and order in the country. We must have order on the highways so that Canada will be leading the van instead of lagging behind the motherland and Germany, France and the United States in coping with this awful death problem.
This is not a party matter. No one knows who will be the next victim. I may be the next one, some hon. gentleman sitting in this chamber to-day may be a victim, and I would be sorry if any of them were not here next year. I ask them, therefore, to rise in their places and express the views of their respective constituencies. Let them tell us what they think of the law and what, in their opinion, should be done to deal with this terrible menace that is ruining the lives of men, women and children and shattering the homes of the country.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT RESPECTING OPERATION OF MOTOR CARS
speechtext:
In rising
to second the motion I should like to commend the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) for his persistence in pressing this matter and for the eminently thorough and practical manner in which he has presented his arguments in support of the bill. I can add very little of use to what he has said, but there is something that I should like to say.
In my opinion, the provisions for cancellation or suspension of licences are particularly useful. We have tried to deal with the senseless slaughter on the highways to which the hon. gentleman has had reference, and to meet the situation by means of short terms of imprisonment and fines, but our efforts have been entirely fruitless. As my colleague has pointed out, the motor car has become such an integral part of present day life that if we deprive motor owners of the right to use their vehicles as a punishment for offences committed while they are in control of their cars, we are proceeding in a manner which will impress these people, and the only manner which will impress them.
In my view the right to use these extremely dangerous machines is conferred after a very superficial test. Much could be done by more severe regulations along these lines. Practically every accident on the highway is preventable. As a practising lawyer who has had many cases to review, I can say that a careful analysis of almost any accident will

show that it was caused in the first instance by excessive speed and in every instance by failure to take adequate care.
It is a great pleasure to me, therefore, besides being a duty, to speak in support of this bill. I would qualify my remarks on the second reading by saying this: I doubt whether we shall be any further ahead by substituting the words "under the influence of alcohol'' for the word "intoxicated." That is a matter of terminology, and no matter how the condition is described in legislation it is a question which will always present grave difficulty to any tribunal that has to pass upou it. In the main, however, the bill is an excellent one, is much needed legislation, and I hope it will receive the support of the house.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT RESPECTING OPERATION OF MOTOR CARS
speechtext:
I have given a vefy great deal	of	consideration and	thought	to	thenumber of accidents that are occurring on our highways, with loss of life, through motor cars.	I	fancy that every	member	of	the
house has done so, and I doubt if there is any of us who has not had occasion to regret the loss of a friend suddenly through some accident of the sort. I recall so many instances; I recall one in which, only a few hours before, I was talking to a young woman, who was going away happily, and then I took up the newspaper and found that she had been killed at a street corner in an accident which, of course, might have been prevented.
The question before us is a very simple one: Shall we make a criminal offence, punishable in the manner indicated in this bill, of violation of a statute which we are about to create with respect to accidents of this kind? Frankly, I think we should. I think the time has come when we can no longer permit laxity of control to prevail in Canada.
Dealing with a matter of principle, here we have to consider the question of restraining young people from driving cars. Now, I have had occasion, as I doubt not every member of this chamber has had, to regret seeing young persons driving motor cars. A motor car weighs very frequently two tons; it seldom weighs less than a ton or a ton and a half. Practically any one of them, however small it may be, will weigh over a ton-I refer to those used in this country. It is true that motor cars weigh less than that in the old country, the small Morris car for instance. To entrust a child of eleven, twelve, thirteen, or fifteen or sixteen years of age, boy or girl, with a machine of that kind upon the highway, is in itself a lack of prudent caution on the part of those who have control of these children. See what it

Criminal Code-Motor Cars
means. The momentum with which that body will strike any given person or machine is obtained by multiplying the rate of speed by the weight. If it is going at only ten miles an hour, one gets some understanding of the tremendous momentum with which it strikes any person who may be in the way of its movement forward. Can we afford as custodians-we are custodians in a large sense of the safety of the public of this country, in that sense at any rate-can we afford to permit this thing to continue, to have these people driving cars?
The second principle is the suspension of the licence. We have not been doing that in this country to the extent which we should. You may say that the provinces can deal with this, but the provinces cannot adequately deal with the question of the criminal character of the offence, and it should not be a law that applies only to one province, it should be universal and passed by this dominion. In England, where of course they have cne law, there is a certain well known peer who drives a car very rapidly. He has had his licence suspended for a year's time. The other day they suspended for life the licence of one who under the influence of intoxicants was driving his car at a high rate of speed, resulting in injury but not death. There is only one way in which you can make control effective in this country, and that is by an amendment to the criminal code; because it is useless to talk about making it effective in Ontario and not in Nova Scotia. We must have a law applicable to the whole dominion. I know of no better field in which you can utilize the criminal law than in that very field. After all should it not be a crime thus to endanger human life? We have our criminal code filled with sections dealing sometimes with mischief, sometimes with conspiracy, sometimes with various small matters, but we have never been hesitant in declaring that any offence against the safety of human life should be regarded as a crime. Is it not the duty of this parliament now to take adequate steps to safeguard those who are travelling on the streets of our country on foot? The House of Lords held-and I commend to my friends in this chamber the reading of Lord Buckmaster's judgment-that it is the pedestrian who has the right of way, not the machine. I can never forget seeing, when passing through the village of Ipswich after that decision, a mother with her child saunter across the street just as leisurely as was possible, while the motor cars had to slow down and wait while she went over. Pedestrians have the right of way. Tell me, Mr. Speaker, to what extent have pedestrians the right of way in Canada? Ask yourselves
that question. All of us know what it is to dodge out of the way of motor cars in this country. They drive by with as much nonchalance and complacency as though they owned the road and we were trespassers. Has not the time come to assert ourselves and say that people who thus endanger human life have committed a crime-because in my judgment it is endangering human life and should be made a crime.
I think this statute is not sufficiently stringent with respect to the suspension of licences. I should like to have it provided in the sections which follow that after the first offence the licence be suspended for a period of years, and I should like to go as far as having it suspended for life. That is the only way that my safety can be secured. Let us be personal and selfish about it; what right has the Minister of Justice to have his life endangered, when he crosses the street to-night, by someone who says, To the blank with him; we are going to drive our car as we see fit. It is a dark night, he is struck; the driver leaves him dying and rushes on. That happens in this country; you only have to read the daily press to see it.
The figures given by the hon. member for Broadview as to the number of deaths resulting in Great Britain, Germany, the United States, Canada, are simply appalling. Think of 37.000 people being killed in the United States in 1935. There are communities in the United States that you and I have been in where we have to dodge to get across the street without being hit by a motor car. We know of one city in particular in Europe where the pedestrian has to risk his life any time he tries to cross the street. Is it not time we should intervene, and should we not intervene in the public interest.
As to the question of those driving cars under the influence of liquor, I think nothing except the most powerful punishment will have any effect. WThen two or three men are tied up in penitentiary for a year or two for driving motor cars while under the influence of liquor it will have the effect of stopping them. I wonder how many hon. members have seriously analysed the number of accident cases that are referable to drink. I confess I have. I have been appalled to find that nearly all the fatal accident cases may be attributed to drink. I am sorry to say that, but it is true. Carry your minds back to these things. I am not referring to that terrible accident where those driving the car were under age; I am referring to the class of cases that make the second branch of what I have to say, namely the class in which accidents occur by reason of the drivers being under the influence
Criminal Code-Motor Cars

of alcohol. The question of defining when a man is intoxicated has always been a matter of great difficulty. For instance, habitual drunkenness is defined and interpreted in a recent English Statute. The question of intoxication has usually been regarded as a matter of proof, and it is for the jury or the judge, as the case may be, to draw the inference from the evidence as to whether or not the person was under the influence of intoxicants so as to be deprived of the power of control which is essential in the driving of a machine such as a motor car.
Laws, Mr. Speaker, are of two kinds; at least there are two phases in which we can consider them. One is the punitive effect, that is, the punishment of the offender; the other is the deterrent effect. If we enact a provision of this kind I submit we shall produce a salutary effect upon drivers of motor cars; it will operate as a deterrent against men going out to drive cars while under the influence of liquor. I believe that. It has been my experience with respect to law and its administration. I am confident that the deterrent effect of a statute of this kind is not easy to over-estimate. AVhy? Because it has behind it a sound body of public opinion. One of the main reasons why sometimes some laws are better enforced than others is that you have behind them an enlightened and powerful public opinion. I am satisfied that the public opinion of this country demands that we should make it punishable, severely punishable, if you will, to drive a motor car under the influence of liquor.

subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT RESPECTING OPERATION OF MOTOR CARS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT RESPECTING OPERATION OF MOTOR CARS
speechtext:
That being so, let us gtapple with this matter and not offer any apologies with respect to it. It is all right to say that the provinces have laws; so they have. But the criminal code is another thing altogether. It applies from coast to coast; it puts all provinces on an equality; it makes possible the punishment of the man in one part of the country equally with the man who lives in another part. In my judgment it leaves the whole situation in a proper perspective with respect to the risks involved and the danger incurred when you have a motor car under the control of one who has been using intoxicants improperly.
The question whether or not a jury may return a verdict on a manslaughter charge for culpable negligence has long engaged the attention of those who are familiar with the development of criminal law. Manslaughter is of course based upon the assumption that there has been culpable negligence, but juries are human and prone (to say: We will not

convict our friend of manslaughter; it is a terrible thing to contemplate, but when the alternative is put to them in the form indicated by this bill, a conviction for culpable negligence, you have a situation of an entirely different character. I do believe that the count for culpable negligence in an indictment would do much to make punishment of the offenders secure and possible where now they escape. All of us unfortunately know, Mr. Speaker-and perhaps it is to the credit of human nature-how difficult it is for a jury of men to sit down and say that their neighbour is to be found guilty of manslaughter. They find it difficult to believe that he was so oblivious to what was going on and so absolutely unconcerned that he did not take proper care, and that manslaughter was the result. But you ask them whether or not they are ready to convict for culpable negligence and that sounds different. That does not sound so bad. After all he may have been just a bit negligent in his job. He may have become careless; he may have been lighting his cigarette or his cigar; he may have failed to take those steps which a man should take to ensure the safety of the passer-by on the street or the highway. If he has done so it seems to me that the question of making it possible to find a verdict of culpable negligence, when the charge of manslaughter is too offensive in the mind of the jury, should be a matter with which we should deal.
There remain only two other matters in the bill that need be mentioned at all. One has to do with the functions of judge and jury. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that it was the act of a great jurist in Great Britain that decided that it was for the jury to come to a conclusion on the question of libel or no libel. Now the question of fact for the jury to determine is as indicated in this section which is part of the bill. It should always, it seems to me, be a matter of fact to be determined by the judge if sitting as judge and jury, and by the jury where there is a jury.
I should like to add just one word more, with regard to the question of impounding motor vehicles. I have not been practising my profession, except to read the cases, for over ten years. One of the last cases in which I was engaged concerned a motor car, a new Cadillac, which came from the province of British Columbia into the province _ of Alberta laden with liquor, in contravention of the provisions of the Alberta act. The government of the province seized the car

Criminal Code-Motor Cars
and the liquor. The magistrate convicted the accused of an offence under the statute and confiscated the car.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE

speechtext: Was it under the criminal code?

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subtopic: PROPOSED AMENDMENT RESPECTING OPERATION OF MOTOR CARS
speechtext:
No, under the liquor act. I think one prosecution was under the criminal code and the other under the liquor act, but of course it was under the liquor act that they confiscated the car as well as the cargo of liquor. I was entrusted by the government of Alberta to deal with the matter and ultimately the case went to the privy council, where it was decided that it was properly confiscated.
If we confiscate a car in the province of Alberta because it contains liquor coming from British Columbia to Alberta, what would you think about simply confiscating a car that kills a man? What would you think about making automobile drivers understand that this sort of thing is not going to be tolerated any longer in Canada? What would you think about making it clear to the man who has eight or ten thousand dollars invested in a car, "You are running the risk of losing that eight or ten thousand dollars by your carelessness, by your negligence, by your disregard of the rules that ordinarily should govern the conduct of men." Sometimes-I am sorry to say this, Mr. Speaker-the measure of carelessness is the measure of newly acquired wealth that enables a car to be purchased costing a large sum of money. That is a very terrible thing to say, but some of us have seen newly acquired wealth express itself in very expensive cars, and drive by with such an entire and utter disregard of the convenience of others; whether it splash them with dirty water from the street or hurl them into the ditch is a matter of profound indifference.
Should we not take steps to stop it? We have the power. We should not leave it to the provinces to deal with it, so that one does and the other does not; we should make it of universal concern in Canada to see that this thing is stopped and that the man whose car brings about this result is punished. It has been part of the law in England from the very start of things, and it is the law upon which was based that old theory of the deodand, that anything that brought about the death of a subject could be destroyed or forfeited; confiscated, as we say sometimes. Forfeited to the crown is the other expression. It was amazing what excellent cars the -11952-35
province of Alberta did get by reason of its confiscation of those automobiles, for the purpose of carrying on its ordinary business, without having to buy them. It was an amazing thing. If, for instance, the mounted police and others of our organizations that require motor cars had them provided at the expense of some of these negligent persons I think it would be a very salutary lesson on the one hand and a very easy way to get motor cars on the other. It might be worthy of consideration; I am sure the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) would be interested.
I do not desire, sir, to take up the time of this house with any further observations. I suggested to the minister that I might speak before he did; not that I think I can in any sense influence his judgment. Far be it from me to assume any such thing as that, but I know how judicial will be his approach to this difficult problem, and the observations I make are expressed in the hope that as he does approach it he will realize that any action he takes to bring about the results which are indicated by this bill will, I believe, meet with the warm approval not only of the members of this chamber but of that great public outside the chamber who are running the risk every day of having their lives taken from them by the carelessness, the indifference and sometimes the drunkenness of those who have these machines under their control.
Mr. DENTON MASSEY (Greenwood); Mr. Speaker, I had not planned to speak on this bill but, having listened to the three excellent speeches which have preceded mine, I am convinced that there is a point which is of the greatest importance and upon which as yet no comment has been made. Accordingly I am taking the liberty of speaking before the right hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) in order to direct his attention to it, so that he may incorporate it in his reply, a matter which seems to me to be fundamental in connection with the principle of this bill.
I listened with a great deal of interest, as I always do, to my colleague and neighbour the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), and I congratulate him, as I do the hon. member for London (Mr. Betts) and my right hon. leader (Mr. Bennett), who followed, on their approach to this matter, endorsing most heartily what they had to say. On the other hand it seems to me that the bill under consideration at the moment fails to go far enough and stops really far short of the point which I think should be reached. The bill deals with effect rather than with cause.

Criminal Code-Motor Cars

By that I mean, who are driving cars? Who get licences to drive cars? How do we know that those who are driving cars are qualified to do so? The hon. member for Broadview referred to the record that had been achieved in Great Britain, the lowering of the number of accidents occurring each day or each year, if you like.
Those of us who have visited the United Kingdom recently have seen attached to licence plates a white plate bearing the red letter "L", indicating that the one in charge of the car is a "learner" or a probationer as an automobile driver. He has applied for his licence and has come up to certain qualified standards, and from then on for, I believe, at least the period of a month, and in some cases as long as three months, he must carry the learner's plate on the rear of his car. This indicates to all and sundry that he is not as yet a qualified driver, and to look out for him. He is not permitted to drive alone at any time during the learner probationary period. He must have accompanying him one who is the holder of a full licence.
I think all who have had experience in driving cars in Canada realize that both on our highways and in our cities there are drivers who are by no means intoxicated, but who act as if they were. I have seen signs on the back of cars which read, "Look out; I may do something foolish." That seems to be one of the best signs which could be attached to some cars I have seen. All hon. members must realize that, as the hon. member for Broadview said, in the vast majority of cases it takes two to make an accident. We have all had the experience where the driver in front of us or the driver coming in from our right or left, or the driver coming towards us, has done something extraordinarily foolish, which has manifested to us the fact that he did not understand the control of a motor car.
There are people driving motor cars to-day -we all know them-whose vision is impaired. There are those who are colour blind, who cannot tell a red light from a green one. There are others who are entirely unfamiliar with the mechanical operation of any machine, let alone an automobile. They know that if they press forward their left foot, shift the lever, and press the right foot as they let go with their left-so far as one can let go of one's foot-the chances are the car will start. After that, heaven alone knows what will happen. Yet, for one reason or another they have been able to convince someone that they are qualified drivers of

motor cars and are then permitted to take charge of their cars, and proceed through our cities and on our highways.
I know that at the moment the granting of driving permits is in the jurisdiction of the provinces, and for a permit to drive a car, one applies to an official in his own province. Notwithstanding anything that has been said so far in regard to drunken drivers, and all that it implies, or in regard to reckless drivers, and all that that implies, it seems to me the fundamental cause of accidents throughout the country is the fact that so many who are driving cars are not qualified drivers in fact, but only in name.
It seems to me that as we have here a national menace, the granting of licences should be a federal function, and could come under the control of federal regulation and law, rather than have the granting of licences left to the individual provinces. Perhaps control might be under the criminal code, or whatever statute would be suitable.
Let me illustrate. Let it be assumed that the laws of British Columbia are extremely strict in the matter of examination for a driving permit, whereas the laws of, say the neighbouring province of Alberta may be less strict. I do not know what the conditions are in those provinces, and I use them simply in a hypothetical case. Yet the man who receives a licence in the province where the requirements are not rigid can go to the province where the requirements are rigid and drive with just as much freedom as he would have in his own province.
Therefore we have here a national question. Implied in the bill is the desire to curtail accidents, and to reduce them to a minimum. When I say that the bill has touched upon the effect rather than the cause I mean that we have left out the most important single facts in the whole question. Therefore I would heartily recommend to the minister that in addition to what is covered by this bill he might give consideration to what I have just suggested, and turn his mind to the question whether or not it is possible, or if you like, within the jurisdiction of the criminal code, to make it criminal to drive a car without adequate knowledge of it, and without being fully capable of so doing.
One more word and I shall have finished. Those of us who have been in the United Kingdom recently have realized that they have gone a long way in traffic regulation through what is called "controlled" and "decontrolled" areas. In certain areas, or rather along certain stretches of highway, one sees the now familiar signs and realizes that he

Criminal Code-Motor Cars
is not under any circumstances permitted to drive over thirty miles an hour. Then along other stretches he sees other now familiar signs, bearing different markings, and he knows there he can drive at any speed, provided he does not drive recklessly. The combination of "decontrolled" and "controlled" areas, along with the new requirements for the gaining of a licence in great part have brought about the substantial lowering of the number of accidents noted in the United Kingdom.
Then, further, our highway laws vary from province to province. To drive in one province under one set of laws, and bo drive in another under another set, is confusing to the traveller. Who knows, as he travels from province to province, or even from town to town, whether he can turn to the right on a red light or whether he cannot. He does not know whether he may drive at only thirty miles an hour on a highway or whether he may travel at fifty. It is all very well bo say that no one should proceed from one province to another without fully acquainting himself with the various laws in the various provinces. But, after all, we are approaching the stage when a trans-Canada highway will be an actuality rather than a politician's dream, and probably we can think about driving from one end of the dominion to the other, through the nine provinces.
Surely when we consider the awful toll that is being taken upon human life, not only in cities but on our highways, a toll not only due to intoxicated drivers or reckless drivers, but partly as a result of drivers without adequate skill to drive a car at all, a lack of knowledge of the machine itself and a lack of knowledge of the traffic laws in the provinces, it must be realized-and I am quite sure my right hon. friend will agree with me-that there should be some dominion-wide, common code which could be recognized as the highway code of this whole dominion. Perhaps that is not easily accomplished. I can readily understand that the right hon. gentleman will see many hazards in the way of each of those matters, but I think that when we consider the bill we should also consider the matters I have mentioned, in addition t,o that which already has been so ably said by hon. gentlemen who have spoken before me.

the holidays a citizen in my district drank a bottle of beer. He and the group with which he was associated were having a picnic in the afternoon and he was driving his car. I should like to find out the cause of our accidents.

speechtext: I know that some men are allowed to drive cars who are thinking of two or three things at the same time. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say just a few words on this bill, from another angle. Many members have spoken from different angles, but I do not think anyone has so far touched on the cost to the public as a result of these accidents. The large increase which has taken place in the number of injuries and accidental deaths over the past ten or fifteen years has had a very considerable effect in raising insurance rates in respect to the automobile. One must realize that insurance is a cooperative proposition; therefore it affects every individual, and if we are to continue to have more deaths and injuries from automobile accidents we are going to have increasingly higher rates of insurance.
Some twenty years or so ago, in the list of the causes of death under life insurance policies over a period, it used to be that diseases of the heart and arteries stood first in the causes of death; next came cancer, and down in the ninth or tenth place, accidents. But gradually over a period of years, due to higher
Criminal Code-Motor Cars

speed and so on, and the increasing number of accidents which took place, we find that while diseases of the heart and arteries still stand in the first place, with cancer next, the third most prevalent cause of death to-day is accidents, and the increase in the number of deaths from accidents is practically all accounted for by the automobile. Despite the fact that preventive medicine has had such a tremendous effect in increasing the average span of life, automobile accidents are counteracting that benefit to a great extent, and life insurance is not getting the benefit of a decrease in the number of deaths generally. If we do not do something about these accidents, life insurance premiums may have to go up. Certainly they will not decrease as they should, and that affects everybody.
There is one other matter to which I should like to refer. I do not think it is the habitual drinker who is causing these accidents and deaths; I believe it is the man who takes drinks only now and then. These occasional drinks speed him uip. Speed is another factor that is contributing to the increase in the number of automobile accidents-speed out of all proportion to the safety of road traffic. I certainly shall endorse this bill.
