speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there seems to be a strong consensus of opinion in this chamber as well as outside in favour of some tightening of the law against reckless driving on the public highway. I am in sympathy with the general principle of the bill that has been submitted by the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), and I also agree with most of the sentiments which have been expressed here this afternoon.
In addition to the many causes that have been given for the higher mortality on the public highway, there is one other which perhaps I should mention. It is that our public highways to-day are used more and more for the transportation of goods, as well as for providing services between various communities in this dominion. The transportation of goods over the public highways between towns and cities and provinces to me is a matter of great concern, and I have no doubt that this traffic contributes to a very large degree in creating conditions of greater danger on the public highway. We find these great vehicles constantly on the highways, creating a hazard which never existed before, and I have in mind the vehicles that are used by both individuals and corporations. It is not uncommon to find on the public highway to-day a heavy vehicle itself weighing many tons, carrying a load
[Mr. D. G. Ross. I
of eight or ten tons, and often it will have one or two, and sometimes three, trailers behind it.
In connection with this transportation of goods a question arises which does come under our jurisdiction, and that is the question of the welfare of the men who are hired to drive that kind of vehicle. I have no doubt that the companies engaged in this kind of business select the best men they can get, but it is not uncommon for these men to be out with a vehicle for long hours at a stretch. They may be out for ten or twelve or fourteen hours at a stretch. While the man may not be driving the truck all that time, nevertheless he is on duty indirectly for the whole of that period, and a man who has been out with a truck or other vehicle for eight or ten or twelve hours at a time is no longer in a fit condition to drive on the public highway. This in itself creates a greater hazard both for the trucks on the highway and for traffic in general.
I realize that the granting of these licences is exclusively a matter of provincial jurisdiction; nevertheless I feel that in view of the number of accidents on the highway and in the interests of the individuals themselves, something should be done by tightening the existing law to make the punishment fit the crime at least in some instances. A driver who has been found guilty of driving a truck or car while under the influence of liquor should not be allowed to drive on the public highway for quite a long time. He should not be allowed to drive a truck or any other vehicle, and in addition the car he was using should be impounded for a certain length of time. That would be one safeguard for the public. I do not drive a ear myself, and so I can speak perhaps more freely.
I hope that the minister in dealing with this question this afternoon, and after attempting to gauge what public feeling is in the matter, will not take a negative attitude in regard to this bill. His department, I have no doubt, has been engaged in studying this question for some time, and I hope that he will give his general approval to the principle underlying this bill in order that we may take in this house steps which will tend to make traffic on the highways much safer than it is at the present time.

speechtext:
I have driven many thousands of miles, in many provinces, in several countries, and under all manner of circumstances, and I have a great deal of sympathy for the average motorist and for the administrators of the various laws governing behaviour on the highways. I know there are many avoidable accidents as well as

Criminal Code-Motor Cars
some that are unavoidable. I know also that the demand for speed and the construction of automobiles with tremendous acceleration, power and high velocity appeal to something in my nature that makes me behave differently in an automobile and on a highway than I would do in a drawing room. I speak simply as an experienced automobile driver, and I say that I do not believe laws can be passed to make people courteous and considerate of the rights and privileges of others. In a matter of this kind, where the safety of life and limb is involved, the deterrent effect of these proposed amendments to the criminal code appeals to me, and I feel that the matter should be effectively dealt with, and not lightly dismissed. If this particular bill is not passed, some measure having at least the same effect should be substituted for it.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext:
May I say immediately that it is my intention to introduce a bill to amend the criminal code, which will be rather extensive, containing alterations of many sections; that not only the proposal of the hon. member who introduced this bill (Mr. Church) but the various suggestions which have been made this afternoon by the speakers will be carefully and duly considered and weighed, and that we shall try to carry out any proposal which is possible and which comes under our jurisdiction, if there is some improvement to be made.
This has been a very interesting discussion, although to some extent a painful one. There is no doubt that the number of deaths caused by motor accidents in Canada is appalling, and that the progress of the motor car levies a heavy toll upon the lives of our fellow citizens. It is the same and even worse in other countries.
The sponsor of this bill has referred to a debate in the British house on this very question, in the month of December. I have read that debate, which any hon. member can see in Hansard of the House of Lords of December 8, and I find from the interesting discussion which took place there, that they are far from considering that the state of the criminal law is the cause of the numerous accidents which happen in the United Kingdom. Indeed, among the matters incident to the discussion, speakers dwelt, for instance, on the consideration that their roads had not been built primarily for the use of motor cars. They spoke of curves, and so forth, and it was suggested that, even at the cost of millions of pounds, the roads should be rebuilt, it being thought that was the main
cause of the accidents. They discussed the question of regulations, of an examination, for example, every year when a driver comes to renew his licence.
The point which the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) has just raised, of competent drivers who are compelled to work for too long hours, also may be relevant to the cause of accidents. But these matters can not very well be dealt with under the criminal code. In the British parliament, of course, they control all that, while here in Canada the provinces control the roads, the licences, and the age of the drivers. I shall consider the subject carefully, but I am free to confess that if a province enacts a statute that the minimum age at which a person may receive a licence shall be sixteen years, or seventeen years, or eighteen years, we cannot legally by an amendment to the criminal code make it a crime. I am not convinced that this parliament can take such action. However, the question is so tremendously important that I am willing to consider everything which has been suggested to-day, to see whether there is not a possibility of making some progress towards doing away with at least part of the evil. I do not know that even a conference as between the provinces to come to some sort of uniformity in the regulations would be effective; that, as suggested by my hon. friend Mr. Massey-I always forget his constituency-

With regard to subsection 7 of section 3 it is proposed that:
Any person who, by the operation or use of any vehicle in a culpably negligent manner, but not wilfully or wantonly, occasions the death of another person, shall, upon conviction, be liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three months or to a fine of not more than one hundred dollars, or to both.
Section 951 of the criminal code provides:
Every count shall be deemed divisible; and if the commission of the offence charged, as described in the enactment creating the offence or as charged in the count, includes the commission of any other offence, the person accused may be convicted of any offence so included which is proved, although the whole offence charged is not proved; or he may be convicted of an attempt to commit any offence so included.
Subsection 3 reads:

maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95

speechtext:
Mr. A. W. NEILL (Comox-Alberni) moved the second reading of Bill No. 11, respecting Japanese immigration.
He said: As I explained on the first reading of the bill, the purport of it is to place Japanese immigration into Canada on exactly the same plane, neither higher nor lower, as that occupied by the Chinese since 1923 when their immigration was last dealt with.
Ever since British Columbia joined confederation the question of oriental immigration and their penetration into every phase of life and industry in that province has been a consideration and an ever-increasing problem for us to deal with there. As far back as 1875 we find the province of British Columbia passing an act forbidding orientals to have votes. At that time the oriental

Japanese Immigration
immigration was entirely Chinese; there were no Japanese. At this point I might follow to its conclusion the history of Chinese immigration, as I want to use it as a parallel to what we should do in connection with the Japanese. Large numbers of Chinese were brought in to build the Canadian Pacific Railway. Their competition in the labour market attracted the ill-will of the labour element, and on representations made the dominion government first in 1885 imposed a poll tax, or an entrance fee if you like, of $50 per head. In 1901 that was increased to S100 and. in 1904, to $500 on every Chinaman entering Canada. It did not apply to Japanese. It was intended to restrict Chinese immigration, but it was not effective. There may have been a temporary check, but it did not amount to anything. It did lead to an undesirable condition, little if at all better than peonage, because large Chinese financial companies would put up the S500 and the man's fare and would proceed to retrieve their money by a lien on the wretched man's wages. That has been done away with for fifteen years, but I am told that there are still Chinamen contributing out of their scanty earnings to repay these big companies which financed their entry into Canada.
Without going into the methods that led to it I will say shortly that in 1923 we passed chapter 95, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927. and I might quote briefly its provisions. From beginning to end it does not use the word "exclusion"; it simply says that entry into Canada is confined to the following classes of people of Chinese origin or descent, then naming the classes: the diplomatic service and those connected with them; children born in Canada going away for their education; merchants and students. That is all. No labour immigration whatever is allowed. And merchants and students are strictly limited; they have to have a passport issued by the Chinese governmeint and visaed by our agent in China. The result has been-it may suit some to say that it is not total exclusion but to all intents and purposes it is total exclusion of Chinese, which it was intended to be. It has worked well, cured a long-standing sore, and there has been no ill-will or dissension or discontent among the Chinese so excluded, with only one exception; they resent and will continue to resent the fact that we have discriminated against them in favour of the Japanese, because we allow a certain number of Japanese to come in. The Chinese also have their pride and do not like this.
Now I have before me the last report of the department of immigration, issued a few days ago. It shows that during the last fiscal year one Chinese immigrant and three students were admitted. And they have a system of allowing Chinese in on temporary permits; missionaries, professors and people like that can come in for a short period, generally six months. Forty-two such permits were issued, and more than half, in fact the bulk of those so admitted, had left Canada within the fiscal year. Chinese went home under circumstances such that they would never be allowed to come back to the number of 1.362. So you can imagine that the Chinese population is rapidly disappearing. Among those that are left the birth rate is very small, because the women are few in number; it only amounts to 5.7, so, that matter is settled.
I have in my hand a report issued by the British Columbia government, prepared by the research department of the economic council, they appear to have been very capable thorough scientific men and their conclusions have been justified by time. They say that in the years 1938 to 1940 inclusive there will be an approximate decrease-note that-of 452 Chinese males thrown upon the labour market. Later on I shall tell you what the effect will be as regards Japanese labour coming on the market, it is a very different story. The Chinese who are left here are treated with respect, they are generally merchants carrying on trade between the two countries, and there is no ill will between us at all with the single exception which I have mentioned.
Coming now to the Japanese, a very different tale must be unfolded. We have a weird thing called a gentleman's agreement with the Japanese. We have had it for many years. It was preceded in 1907, or possibly 1906, by riots in the streets of Vancouver; feeling then as now was running very high-I think it is more intense now- there were riots; I think the Japanese consulate was stoned and windows broken. The Hon. Mr. Lemieux, our late lamented Speaker, was sent to Japan to negotiate what was called a gentleman's agreement. I should like to quote from the debate which took place on his return. Mr. Macpherson, then the member for Vancouver, speaking in the debate, as reported at page 2087 of Hansard of 1907-08, said:
They-
That is, the then government.
-have carried on negotiations with Japan which have resulted in stopping for all time any further influx of Japanese coolies into our country.
Japanese Immigration

Mark that! And I suppose Mr. Mac-pherson believed what he said. But Mr. Sproule said, "How do you know?"
Mr. Macpherson: I will tell my hon. friend how I know. The Minister of Labour has just come back from Japan and he has stated in parliament upon his responsibility as a minister of the crown, that we need never fear any further immigration from Japan. That statement has been accepted by the house; that statement has been accepted by the country.
Mr. Sproule: No.
Mr. Macpherson: My hon. friend says, no.
Mr. Sproule: The hon. gentleman says that statement is accepted by the house and by the country. Had we not years ago a similar statement from the government that the Japanese would regulate immigration, and yet the Japanese government have not regulated immigration to the satisfaction of even the hon. member himself?
He then speaks of a period "four or five years ago," that is, four or five years precedent to 1907 or 1908. So that between thirty-five and forty years ago we were told this old love story, that we could trust the people of Japan and everything would be lovely. And now conditions are worse than they were then.
I think we are the only country in the world, at least we are the only dominion that has an arrangement with Japan which allows labourers to come in. Some of them have gentleman's agreements, but none to let labour come in. Here I Should like to allude to- I do not want to use a harsh word so I will say the secrecy that has always been allowed to cover up and put a smoke screen around this gentleman's agreement. That is one of the worst features of it. I find that in 1908, the Hon. Mr. Lemieux was speaking and he gave a short statement as to what this gentleman's agreement was. It was the most vague and indefinite thing you can conceive. Let me quote the sense of it. I refer to page 1610 of Hansard of January 21, 1908. This is from a letter signed by a Japanese statesman -I do not know what his title was-addressed to Mr. Lemieux:
Acting in this spirit and having particular regard to circumstances of recent occurrence in British Columbia,-
That is the riots.
-the imperial government-
That is the Japanese government.
-have decided to take efficient means to restrict emigation to Canada. In carrying out this purpose, the imperial government, in pursuance of the policy above stated, will give careful consideration to local conditions prevailing in Canada, with a view to meeting the desires of the government of the dominion as far as is compatible with the spirit of the treaty and the dignity of the state.
That is the Japanese state. Well there is nothing very definite about that. Someone
	-
had the temerity to ask in the house just what was to be done: "Will the hon. minister tell the house to what extent the Japanese government promised to restrict emigration?" Mr. Lemieux replied:
My hon. friend is too inquisitive. I will not answer, not from disrespect for him, but because if I did answer I would commit an act unworthy of a Canadian representative and unworthy of myself.
Because he had agreed to various unknown, unstated things; he talks about stringent regulations and then refuses to give the information to the house. Then he says:
There is, however, one feature of these regulations *which I am authorized to make public.
Then he refers to restriction of immigration; but it is all up in the air, in the clouds, and as we afterwards found out it stayed in the clouds. The result was that although the thing was supposed to be in existence, nobody knew anything about it. I once asked an immigration official this question: "If the Japanese gentleman's agreement calls for only four hundred a year"-for that is what it did at the time-"why did seventeen hundred come in last year?" The answer I got was, "I don't know. I have never seen the gentleman's agreement, and when a fellow comes along and says he is coming in under the gentleman's agreement, we allow him to come in because we do not know anything to the contrary." There was an entire lack of what you might call fixity as to what the thing was or what it meant.

speechtext:
It was along about 1917, as far as my memory serves me. but the figures were always exceeded. The gentleman's agreement was not a gentleman's agreement; it was a gentleman's joke as far as one party to the bargain was concerned.
We are talking about a gentleman's agreements. I have in my hand a gentleman's agreement about which there is no secrecy. This is a white paper, which corresponds to our Canadian blue-books, issued by the government of South Africa. Here is the gentleman's agreement made with Japan, all above board; here they say who are to be allowed

Japanese Immigration
in, and who are not: 1. Tourists; 2. Persons visiting the Union solely for the purpose of study or scientific investigation; 3. Wholesale merchants and buyers of South African produce for export as well as their respective staffs; 4. The wives and children of any person admitted under paragraphs 1. 2 and 3. That is all. There was no labour immigration there; no permanency, because the agreement continues:
The permits issued under this understanding shall be for one year-
And they were renewable at the option of the government. To make it quite clear that South Africa was to remain a white Africa, this further clause was added:
Children born to any such person during such temporary domicile shall have no claim in consequence to Union nationality, birthright or domicile.
That is a very fine gentleman's agreement; it is above board, for all to read and understand, and there is no labour immigration involved at all. It simply covers, as I have said, the diplomatic service, tourists, scientists, wholesale merchants and their wives and children.
However, we got a gentleman's agreement, such as it was. It proved to be Dead sea fruit as far as we were concerned, partly due to the secrecy involved and partly due to the necessarily loosely worded agreement made between two gentlemen who, it is expected, will vie with each other to see that they live up not to the letter but beyond the letter of the agreement. It does not work, however, when you make agreements like that and one of the parties is so mentally constituted, probably by tradition and heritage-I do not blame them altogether-that they do not deem it any dishonour to break even a written bargain, as we have seen in recent times, let alone one so vaguely expressed. That was the weak point.
After the war, feeling again ran very high, and in the spring of 1922 the hon. gentleman who now represents Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens), but who then represented Vancouver Centre, called together the British Columbia members. I think that was the first and only time the British Columbia members united about anything. There were four groups represented in that room on that occasion, and we agreed to introduce a resolution asking for the total exclusion of orientals. The government insisted on taking out those
words and putting in " effective restriction," saying that meant the same thing. At page 1573 of Hansard for that session I asked:
Can the leader of the government give us an asurance that, in his mind, the words "effective restriction" in the amendment convey such a measure of restriction as is, at least, equal to the present immigration act in force in Australia to-day?
In Australia at that time they had no gentleman's agreement, or if they had they also had a test by which the Japanese were totally excluded. It was a language test, which I need not go into now. The answer was:
Mr. Mackenzie King:	I have in mind the
same object exactly as the people of the country to which my hon. friend has referred had in mind when they enacted their legislation, namely to have a restriction that will be effective.
The then leader of the opposition, the Right Hon. Mr. Meighen, suggested other words. He said, " Well, if you do not like the word 'exclusion'; if that is offensive to the Japanese, why not use the word ' prohibition '?" When that was not accepted by the government he suggested other words, such as " for residence purposes," but that was not accepted. Then he suggested another phrase, " bringing to an end further such immigration for residence purposes." He made an honest attempt to produce something that would really mean effective restriction, but the government did not accept any of his suggestions and put through their amendment using the words " effective restriction " instead of " total exclusion."
After that our committee of British Columbia members more or less disbanded and lost heart. Three of us carried on, two members from British Columbia who were on the Liberal side at that time, and myself. But we soon found that effective restriction did not mean the same as total exclusion, as carried out in Australia, by any means. However, we got something in 1923; we got the Chinese exclusion act put through, to which I have just referred. It worked well and, as I have said, it would have been all right if only we had included the Japanese as well. We used every influence we possessed and every influence we could influence to try to get the Japanese included as well.
Some of the members who came into the house when I did, in 1921, will remember- some of them have happily and conveniently forgotten-that during the strenuous times of 1922 and 1923 and more particularly 1925 and 1926, the minor groups in the house possessed a great deal more influence in regard to legislation than they do now. Even
Japanese Immigration

the voice of a lone independent was more vibrant before 1926 than it is now that big majorities have become the order of the day. Possibly that is a good thing for the big parties, but I do not know if it is a good thing for the small groups and the people they represent, who are generally what might be called underprivileged or those seeking some social or legislative justice but who are not sufficiently powerful to attract or command the notice and attention of the bigger parties. However, wTe kept on. We got the act respecting the Chinese, and it was a success. I well remember the bitter controversy at that time. The senate was lobbied; we were lobbied, and there was a tremendous uproar over the passing of that act, but there has not been a word of objection since. It was a success; in a word, it worked.
We were denied the same legislation with regard to Japanese. Time went on. My two confreres from British Columbia were defeated, largely because of the attitude of the government they had supported in making these promises and not delivering the goods. I persevered, but it was not until 1928, six years after the promise, that I secured even a measure of fulfilment of that promise with regard to the Japanese. The government of that day amended the gentleman's agreement, and so far as that amendment went I give full credit and thanks to the then Prime Minister, who is also the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). He did two good things. First he cut the number down from 400 to 150. Then, more important, he arranged that the great bulk of these immigrants would come in under the jurisdiction, so to speak, of our Immigration Act and our immigration authorities. That was a very good thing indeed. He also arranged that immigrants had to have their passports visaed in Japan by one of our agents there. It placed the agreement more or less under our control- but only more or less.
Since then the agreement has been in force and I am told-and it is easily ascertainable- that in several cases and, perhaps, in most of the years, less than the quota has come in. Perhaps that has been largely due to the depression and, in later years, due to internal conditions in Japan.
However, the usual loophole has been discovered, as it always has been, and always will be. by which more Japanese have come in under this gentleman's agreement, as it is interpreted. I need not go into it now, but it does permit people to come in that I, at least, never contemplated would be allowed to come in except under the quota. If it came

about that the Japanese were determined to force immigration, they would be able to do it, under the terms of this loophole. The really fatal mistake was in not making the Chinese act of 1923 apply to the Japanese also. The United States had done it, just about that time. They were threatened with tremendous consequences; sabres and swords were waved, but nothing happened. They were threatened with an enormous loss of trade-which would have lasted only two or three months. Trade will always go where trade finds it is best adapted to go, and it does not pay attention to matters of this kind.
If we had done it then we would only have been in line with the other dominions and, so far as 1 know, with other countries as well. The principle has often been laid down to protect the people native to a country against incursions, however legal, of aliens. By the native I do not mean the aborigines alone; they may be natives in the sense of having long occupancy in a country.
In Kenya colony in East Africa the British government, which has control, said they found it necessary to record their considered opinion that the interests of African natives must be paramount, and that if and when those interests and the interests of the immigrant nations conflicted, the former should prevail. That was the view taken by the British government.
Next we find General Smuts in a speech referring to the "warping influence of the fear of ultimate black domination." If we substitute the word "Japanese" for "black" we have described the situation in British Columbia in our own country. He there mentioned the "warping influence of the fear of ultimate black domination."
Mr. K. K. Kawakami, one of Japan's most distinguished publicists, in an article written a few years ago said this:
People accustomed to low wages and therefore a low standard of living can successfully compete with and ultimately defeat people with a higher standard of living.
Sure. Here is the last illustration. I see connected with it the name of Sir Shenton Thomas, the gentleman who opened the Singapore base the other day. He was the governor, or whatever the position is, of the Malay colony. In this case, the Chinese and Indians, who were aliens, came in bringing in capital and dominating industry, and they were beginning to make demands for a place in the sun-jobs in the civil service, and permanent positions like that. He gave them what is described in the article as a cold rebuff when he announced that there would

Japanese Immigration
be no appointments to administrative positions among non-Malay Asiatics. They became angry, and said that much of the development was due to their effort, and so on.
Sir Shenton Thomas said that he did not deny that fact, but argued that the Malayan was in danger of being dispossessed in his own country, and that therefore special measures were necessary for his own protection. Some extensive land reservations which can never pass out of Malayan ownership, and certain non-manual government branches virtually reserved to Malayans, are included in such measures.
That gives an illustration of what I have in mind. But we took the opposite view. Let me quote Mr. Lemieux in this connection. I do not suppose he thought he was making history, when he said, at page 1591 of Hansard for 1908:
The policy of this government has always been to let Japan herself regulate and restrict voluntarily the emigration of her subjects;-
That is, the emigration to Canada-
-any other policy would not have been successful with that nation.
That is the trouble. We have surrendered our right of control of the immigration into our country of the subjects of a foreign nation. There was the initial mistake, and it has endured ever since. That will conclude my observations on this phase of the matter. I would ask that you call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the modified gentleman's agreement of which I spoke before six o'clock, and which came into effect, I think, in September, 1928, had five major bad consequences or effects.
First, it missed a good opportunity of settling once for all a question that was bound to rise up again and again, and be more and more troublesome each time it came up.
Second, being a gentleman's agreement, of very necessity its terms were so slack that it offered large opportunities for evasion. I said, in speaking this afternoon, that the quota had been generally lived up to. Yes, according to the figures you will get over at the immigration department, if you send for them, that is correct.
But this is an instance that came to my notice. It is in a confidential statement, and I cannot give its source, but every name is
given, and I can guarantee- its bona fides. The mounted police had in hand certain fraudulent transactions in connection with birth certificates, and they found that seventy-five Japanese birth certificates had been faked and 117 fishing licences illegally obtained. The Japanese interpreter-and the interpreter is always Japanese, never a white man-went to the penitentiary for two and a half years over that, but I do not suppose there is a member of the house who has ever heard a word of that transaction but myself. Now, if after investigation they managed to find seventy-five such instances, surely we can suppose that at least three times that number actually evaded the regulations. Other members, no doubt, can give similar instances.
In any case, even supposing there is no evasion, the Japanese agreement allows an increase of the adult Japanese population every year in a situation which is already overloaded. I quote again the British Economic Council's report, which was a very valuable document, and time has proved how accurately and carefully it was drawn up. They say that in the years from 1936 to 1940 the increase of Japanese will throw on the labour market 3.874 people, or an average of 774 a year. That was not an increase to the population by way of infants, but the number that would be thrown on to the labour market in those years, and it gives an average -and they itemize it, by both birth and immigration-of 774. That could well be done away with, considering the situation in British Columbia.
The third objection is that in times of depression, when it is necessary to forbid our own white citizens from the British Empire entering this country, and the Bennett government in, I think, 1931 or possibly 1930, passed an order in council seriously restricting the immigration of ordinary labourers from the British Isles, and necessarily so. for the protection of the Canadian working man-

maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext: It is still in force.

maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext:
But at that same time, under the gentleman's agreement, the Japanese could send in their quota, and as much more as they could get away with, in defiance of any immigration order the government had passed. That is the serious objection. It is a wholly untenable and undesirable position for us to be in.
Fourth-and this is one of the major objections-it hands over the control of immigration to the judgment of an alien nation- a thing that is not done anywhere else in the world.

Japanese Immigration
Let me quote from page 2039 of volume 2 of Hansard of 1908, and this is no mere back bencher like myself speaking, but a man whose words are entitled to some respect, the late Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden. He said:
Now I come more particularly to the results of the mission to Japan of my hon. friend the Postmaster General. The real object of his mission was to induce Japan to exercise that control over immigration into Canada which we should be able to exercise ourselves. It is one of the attributes of the sovereign power of any state to restrict, or even altogether prohibit, the entrance of aliens within its territory. If we had preserved that right by the stipulation insisted upon by the Conservative government in August, 1895, there would have been no difficulty. We did not reserve that right; therefore, having passed over to the Japanese government that control which should have been exercised by ourselves, it became necessary for my hon. friend the Postmaster General to go to the Japanese government and to ask them to exercise some control and some regulation.
At another point the same gentleman moved an amendment to this effect to the motion which was before the house, at page 2146 of the same volume of Hansard:
That this house while expressing its profound appreciation of the friendly intentions and courteous assurances of the Japanese government, and while declaring its sincere desire for the most cordial relations with the Japanese people, desires nevertheless to record its strong protest against a policy under which our wageearning population cannot be protected from destructive invading competition except by entreating the forbearance and aid of a foreign government.
The words "wage-earning" might now be taken out and there be inserted instead "the population of British Columbia", because it is no longer the wage-earners' problem, but applies to every industry, high and low, in the province.
Worst of all, the agreement even as amended puts us :n the most invidious position as regards China. China has been a divided nation, and therefore has received perhaps less attention than she should have, but she will come back a unified nation with her four hundred millions of population, with her trained soldiers-I think it was General Gordon who said that the Chinese soldiers were the best in the world-and with her market potentialities of four hundred million purchasers. We will go to China and she will say: You want to trade with us, but why do you treat us so differently from the way you treat the Japanese? And what answer can we give? We shall then be in this position: Either we shall have to reinstate Chinese immigration, which is very unde-
[Mr. Neill.1
sirable, or under the pressure of China's population of four hundred millions and her soldiers we shall have to put the Japanese back where I now seek to put them. If we are going to do it under pressure from China then, why not let us do it now with all the good will that comes from a free will act of justice? Let us do it now rather than under pressure later.
I remember that Mr. Meighen, when the debate was on in 1922, said this:
Let us proceed to argument. I stated first that there had been effective exclusion of the inhabitants of China in the United States. My hon. friend-
That was the then Prime Minister:
My hon. friend says: "Oh, yes, but China is not a first class power."
Then Mr. Meighen continued:
Are we to modify our language according to the number of troops that there may be in the nation to which that language refers? I do not think Japan would expect us to do that; I do not think China would be flattered to know that that is the reason she is excluded.
That is all I have to say about the gentleman's agreement. I have been told that my bill does not go far enough; that it does not touch the biggest feature of all, and I admit it. The biggest feature of all is the enormous birthrate of the Japanese in British Columbia about 38 per thousand as against 18. I have in my hand figures, and I shall give them briefly.
The school enrolment in British Columbia in the ten years 1927 to 1937 went up twelve per cent; the Japanese enrolment went up eighty-eight per cent. These are significant figures; multiply them by the next ten or twenty years and what kind of situation does it present to your mind? The answer is, of course, that we cannot stop their birth rate- unless we are prepared to bring them under the provisions of chapter 258 of the revised statutes of British Columbia-but we can at least stop adult immigration coming in to add to the vicious circle-more immigrants, more children, more men and women thrown on the labour market, and not only the labour market but all industries in British Columbia. Since even 1923 the legal immigration would mean perhaps twenty-three or twenty-five hundred people, all young people with the potentialities of large families. It may be said: Let us deport them. That is impossible. But we can at least stop the legal entry of them, and above all stop the loopholes that seem inevitably to be connected with any gentleman's agreement, however carefully drawn.

Japanese Immigration
I ask support of this bill on its merits, to correct past errors and prevent more. I ask support from hon. members from all over Canada. It may be said that the east has no such problem. I tell hon. members from Quebec province and also those representing the industrial centres of Ontario: It does concern you. It concerns you vitally. Your line of defence against fatally cheap labour competition is not Montreal or Toronto; it is in British Columbia; it may be our trouble to-day, but it is your's to-morrow. If you in Quebec had the oriental population that we have the numbers would be 265,000; in Ontario they would be 312,000. Just where would you be then? Remember they are all of alien thought and mind and tendency; they are all one body, acting and thinking as a unit. Just where would you put 312,000 in Ontario, and how would you like to have them?
I ask support to this bill with no idea, no hint of taking advantage of the popular prejudice on account of what has gone on during the last year or two. I have never mentioned the war. I ask support on a nonpartisan basis. This is not a bill brought down by the government, immediately ipso facto to be opposed by the opposition. It is not brought in by the opposition, immediately to be regarded as suspect by the government, as a device to embarrass them. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) recently said, with reference to a matter brought in by a private member, " It is a good thing to have a frank and sincere consideration of the subject." It may be well said, if we pass this bill, that it is not the act of any party in the house, it is the act of parliament, which is paramount. Therefore, in all sincerity, I ask the support of every member of this house to this bill.

maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext:
In rising to speak in support of this bill I realize that it is difficult for hon. members from the other provinces of Canada to appreciate the situation in British Columbia. I thought this afternoon, as I saw the attention with which the members present in the house were following the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), that it would have cheered the hearts of the people of British Columbia if they could have been in the gallery to notice that attention. Because after all this question of Japanese immigration is of vital importance to our province, and there is no way in which the people of the rest of Canada can win the friendship and gratitude of British Columbians more readily than by listening to their case on this subject of immigration
and helping them to solve the problem. It is a problem which is steadily getting worse; the position has become more serious year after year. I believe I am the only real British Columbian in this house.

maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext: Oh! Oh!

maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext:
Our province is represented by members who were bom in Scotland, in Ireland, in England, and one hon. member, of whom we are very proud, was bom in Sweden; we even have members who were born in Ontario and the maritime provinces; but I am afraid that I am the only one born in British Columbia. Apparently the old adage, "A prophet is not without honour save in his own country," is applicable to that province. However, I mention myself for the reason only that ever since my childhood-and I am sure that most of the younger men and women who were born in British Columbia have had the same experience-this issue has hung over the province like a black cloud, steadily growing larger, the situation steadily getting worse. It would be impossible for my fellow members from other parts of Canada to realize how seriously we treat this matter, and I ask of you to-night that in considering this bill you approach it in a non-partisan and non-political way, as fellow Canadians concerned to solve a difficult problem in a sensible manner.
The real problem with which the people of British Columbia are faced is this:	First of
all, how can oriental immigrants and their descendants be assimilated? That is the basis of the problem. Second, if these oriental immigrants and their descendants cannot be assimilated, then what is to be done with them? It is not only the most serious problem facing British Columbia but also, I suggest, one of the gravest questions facing the people of Canada as a whole.
The first step towards a solution is to stop further immigration. That course was taken many years ago by the other nations which were faced with the same difficulty, for instance, by Australia, New Zealand, and the United States of America. Canada herself went part of the way as far back as 1908, when she nogatiated a gentleman's agreement with Japan limiting Japanese immigrants to approximately 400. Again in 1923, as the hon. member for Comox-Albemi has pointed out so clearly, Canada realized that oriental immigration must be further checked, when she enacted the Chinese Immigration Act. At that time the Chinese population of
Japanese Immigration

British Columbia was far greater than the Japanese population, and the Chinese were coming into the country in far larger numbers than the Japanese. The question of Chinese immigration was more serious than that of Japanese immigration. The parliament of Canada, under our present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) faced that problem and passed the Chinese Immigration Act. The result has been that in the thirteen years following the enactment of that- legislation only eight Chinese immigrants have been admitted to Canada. The government of British Columbia estimates that the Chinese population of that province is falling; that it has dropped approximately five thousand during the last six years, and is now only about twenty-two thousand.
Canada again recognized the principle that further immigration should be stopped, or at any rate should be further checked, when in 1929 the Canadian government negotiated an alteration in the gentleman's agreement with Japan, cutting down the number of immigrants from 400 to 150. But during the thirteen years in which only eight Chinese came into Canada, there were 3,411 Japanese immigrants coming into the country and the Japanese population was growing steadily. Now the British Columbia government estimate that there are approximately 30,000 Japanese in the province, and it is certain that that province has reached the stage where it can absorb no more. The time has come to stop further Japanese immigration.
To show you the attitude of the people of British Columbia I quote from an editorial appearing in the Vancouver Daily Province of February 2, this year. I believe it gives the opinion of practically every one in British Columbia. This editorial reads in part:
We have plenty of room for immigrants, but it is immigrants who are assimilable that we want and the Japanese are not assimilable. We have about 30,000 Japanese in British Columbia, now, and these, with their natural increase, are rather more than we can comfortably handle. All immigration from Asia should be stopped.
There are several features of this Japanese immigration which make it very serious. The first is that practically all Japanese immigrants settle in British Columbia; they do not spread out to the other provinces. For instance, in the last fiscal year 103 were admitted under the gentleman's agreement, and of that number 101 settled in British Columbia, only two settling outside; those two went to Alberta. Over ninety per cent of the Japanese in Canada, reside in British Columbia, whereas of the Chinesse less than sixty per cent reside in our province, the

others being scattered throughout the other provinces, and yet a worse feature is that ninety per cent of the Japanese in Canada are concentrated in the coast area of British Columbia. They are not scattered across the province, but are concentrated along the coast. Just to bring it home to hon. members from other parts of the country I would point out that if the same proportion of the population of Manitoba were Japanese, you would have this picture: there would be 30,000 Japanese settled within a few miles of Winnipeg. That would correspond to the actual settlement about Vancouver. In Ontario, on the same basis, it would mean 150,000 Japanese settled in and around Toronto and central Ontario. In Quebec there would be 120,000 settled, say about Montreal and Quebec and up the St. Lawrence valley. In New Brunswick there would be 17,000 settled around St. John and up the St. John river, and in Nova Scotia there would be 20,000 Japanese settled in and about Halifax. That will give you some idea of the Japanese settlement in British Columbia at the present time.
The second serious feature about this immigration is that there are more women coming in than men, and that has been the situation for many years. For instance, during the last fiscal year there were thirty-nine males and sixty-four females, and on December 31, 1936, the Japanese population of British Columbia consisted of approximately 56-7 per cent males and 43-3 per cent females, the percentage of females having risen from year to year. With the Chinese on the other hand, 90 per cent were males and only 10 per cent females.
The third serious feature is that the birthrate among the Japanese population in British Columbia is far higher than that of any other race. The Japanese birthrate is twenty per thousand; the birthrate of whites in British Columbia is only 13-6 per thousand, and the Chinese birthrate is 6-1 per thousand. This shows that the situation is bound to get worse from year to year.

maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman will find that the Japanese birthrate is higher than that, 36 or 38.

maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext:
Well, it is bad enough. The situation is really this: There is growing up in British Columbia a state within a state. The Japanese people do not intermarry with the whites; and mind you, they are just as much opposed to such intermarriage as the whites are. It is not a question of one race being superior and the other inferior; the simple fact is that intermarriage is not wished by either race. Then there is the question of language. The Japanese even have their own

Japanese Immigration
schools after the regular day school in order that Japanese children born in British Columbia may learn the Japanese language as well as the English.
Again, employment in the industries of the province is seriously affected. For example, in the fishing industry, one of our great industries, there are over 2,000 licences issued to Japanese, and we estimate that there are over 1,200 Japanese fishing boats plying up and down the coast, in and out of our harbours. In order to get licences the Japanese must be naturalized, and I do not think there is any question that in many cases they have taken out naturalization papers just for the purpose of being able to get fishing licences.
There are thousands of Japanese farming, carrying on principally poultry farming and the growing of small fruits; many of them are scattered up the Fraser valley. At the present time hundreds and thousands of prairie people are coming into British Columbia as a result of the drought and they are forced to compete with these Japanese already settled on the land. We have a chance to help the very best settlers any province could wish to have, and yet we are handicapped at every step because there are so many Japanese engaged in the same line of endeavour.
Many of them have gone into the lumber business, into pulp and paper, and into mining, while in the cities on the coast hundreds of them are in business. I have before me a list of the licences issued by the city of Vancouver in the year 1937, showing that there were 795 licences issued to Japanese and 644 to Chinese, covering nearly every line of business. There are fifteen Japanese apartment house proprietors; nine auto repairers; thirty-nine barbers; eight boot and shoe repairers; eighty candy merchants; one hundred and fifteen cleaners and dyers; forty-four dressmakers; eighteen fish dealers; twenty-one greengrocers; one hundred and ten grocers. And I was told shortly before leaving for Ottawa, that there was even a real danger of the Japanese running the chain stores out of the grocery business in Vancouver, from which hon. members can realize what effect they have on the white merchants who are trying to compete with them. There are also seven tailors; one hundred and twenty-nine lodging houses; eleven manufacturers; thirty-two restaurants; fourteen miscellaneous retail stores; seven ;eweliers; twenty-three wholesale dealers; ten express and dray enterprises and many other occupations.
The competition of these immigrants with our white people is absolutely unfair. They have a lower standard of living. Their ways
of living make it frightfully difficult for us to carry out our social security laws. It is very difficult to make them comply with those laws, which means unfair competition for the white people who do try to comply with them. In farming their competition is most unfair, because farm labour immigrants, who have to be placed with Japanese farmers, work for a few dollars a month or a year; no one knows what they get, probably not much more than their board; but the result is that the Japanese farmer with this cheap labour is forcing off the land the white farmer who has to pay proper wages to his men. The same thing is true in fishing, Japanese helping other Japanese. The Japanese merchants in the cities live in the back of the stores, and not having expenses to meet such as the white merchant has, can drive the latter out of a district. It has always been believed, although I cannot prove it, that the Canadian Japanese Association or the Japanese consulate stands behind these men financially when they wish to buy a farm or a fishing boat or go into business, and that they can get capital from such sources at a rate of interest far lower than can be obtained by a white man.
That gives the house a rough picture of the situation. Always we have been met with the statement that we must do nothing which will upset our relations with Japan, but I believe that the Japanese government appreciates our difficulty just as well as we appreciate it ourselves. The Japanese government has on different occasions shown an understanding of the situation; these gentleman's agreements are evidence of that; and I believe that government will realize that this situation is one with which Canada must deal. I think Japan will respect us all the more for facing the problem. I cast no aspersions on the Japanese people or the Japanese government. That nation deserves the greatest credit for what it has done, for the way it has progressed. Probably no nation in the history of the world has done so well in so short a time. The Japanese race are merely different from our race; perhaps in some things they are not as good, in others are better. But our problem is simply the question of whether or not we can assimilate the race in this nation we are trying to build.
In conclusion, I would emphasize again that the need for this legislation is clear, and that now is the time to act. The problem gets more difficult the longer it is put off. There is no reason why parliament should hesitate about these obvious remedies. After all, the Canadian people are a people of courage, of initiative, of sound judgment, and the Canadian parliament should show courage in tack-
Japanese Immigration

ling such problems as this. We boast of being a nation, and this parliament should realize that nationhood involves being able to decide for ourselves what is to be done in Canada. Let us treat this matter as the serious national problem it is, and thereby as well show the people of British Columbia that it is possible for them to have their problems considered here and dealt with, despite the fact that parliament sits three thousand miles away from that great province.

maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext:
The oriental question in British Columbia is one of the most serious questions facing the people of that province to-day. It has come to the front perhaps more during this time of depression than at any other period. I have always held the opinion that Canada maybe was wrong in differentiating as between the oriental races; I believe we should have treated the	Japanese the	same	as we treated	theChinese, and not favoured the people from Japan while excluding the Chinese. The two hon. members who have spoken before me on	this question	have	covered practically
every aspect of the situation, but there are one or two matters upon which I should like to dwell in the short time at my disposal. I say that because later on I intend to deal with this question as it affects the fishing industry in our province, particularly on the Fraser river.
I	wonder how	many	hon members	areaware that the Chinese	who come to	this
country have contributed well over $21,000,000 to the national exchequer. They are practically the only oriental people coming to this country who have had to pay a head tax. From the records of the immigration department I find that from 1885 to 1923, which was the year that the doors were closed to the Chinese, the sum of $21,223,150 was paid by some 82,370 Chinese entering Canada. So I do not think the Japanese have cause to complain that they are being picked upon at this time if our criticism is levelled more at them than at the Chinese. I may point out that the number of Chinese in Canada is getting less, due to the fact that many of them are dying off, and also that only ten per cent of the Chinese in British Columbia are females as against fifty per cent of the Japanese, who, I believe, have a studied policy in connection with their emigration of seeing that enough females go to the various countries along with the males so that the Japanese stock will be maintained in those countries. I wonder how many hon. members are aware that according to the Japanese year book, issued, I assume, under
the authority of the Japanese government, in 1930 over 28,000,000 yen were sent back to Japan by Japanese residents abroad, and that the total number of Japanese abroad in the various countries of the world in 1930 was 634,913. The total for the United States and Canada was given as 120,000. They have gone into practically every country in the world, including Great Britain, where the report shows some 1,500.
I was interested in figures presented by the Japanese delegation which came to Ottawa in 1936, and appeared before the franchise and elections committee. They seemingly came armed with information as to the numbers of their race resident in British Columbia. They told that committee that according to a census taken by themselves there were only some 19,960 resident in that province. Of that number 10,965, they stated, were Canadian born, leaving only some 8,995 who, therefore, must have come into the country. Yet, according to the Japanese year book for 1930, Japan claimed to have over
21.000	resident in British Columbia alone. A careful survey was made in British Columbia by the provincial government and a very conservative estimate of the number in that province would be 30,000.
Mention has been made of the increasing birth rate. It is rather a problem, because the estimated birth rate of the Japanese is between fifty and sixty per thousand as against eighteen per thousand for the white population. If it were worked out in that ratio it would be discovered that even if we closed the gate now-and by the way, I am in favour of that-in twenty-five years there would be
67.000	Japanese in British Columbia.
While I am all in favour of the principle
of the bill, I am afraid that we are just a little late in closing the gate. There is another aspect of the matter, in connection with the number who have come in during the years of the depression. While that number is not as alarming as in years gone by, still it is disturbing indeed to find that Japanese with five or ten acres of land in the Fraser valley can make application, and have been doing so, under the dominion immigration laws to bring in the odd Japanese, presumably to work on the ranch. But if one would follow up that man who is brought in, it would be found that he stays perhaps one month or two months working on the land and then is slipped into industry. It is no wonder that our people are very much perturbed over such a situation, when in many industries they find men from . Japan who

Japanese Immigration
have been here only three or four months but who have found employment while our own people have been walking the streets.
I well remember making the statement in the house in 1931 that there were hundreds if not thousands of citizens of Japan in this country illegally. The then Minister of Immigration-I suppose he had to do it- got up and denied the truth of such a statement. But, Mr. Speaker, I discovered that later on instructions were issued to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to make a careful survey, or as careful as possible, of the situation. Just before I left for Ottawa to attend the present session I was told by the authorities that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police had discovered close to six hundred who had entered this country without papers, surreptitiously, and that nine hundred others had suddenly left the country when they realized that they were going to be checked up by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. That is a serious situation. I was not glad to hear the statement; I mention it here because it substantiates what I said on the floor of the house when I was on the other side of it, that there are hundreds and hundreds of Japanese who entered this country surreptitiously, and we have advocated that perhaps a closer check should be made of their numbers, with a view to finding out exactly who should or should not be in this country. I should like to have serious note taken of the entry of those who come presumably to work on the land but who, after being here one, two or three months, find their way into various industries and compete, and very successfully, with our own people.
My purpose in rising at this time, Mr. Speaker, was to join with the two previous speakers and the sponsor of the bill. I am entirely in accord with the principle contained in this legislation and desire to lend it all the support of which I am capable, although I realize that the matter is not one capable of easy solution. We may, at least, take a step in the right direction.
I am not going to make any extended remarks at present because on the order paper in my name there is a resolution asking for a cut in the number of Japanese fishing licences, and when that resolution is under discussion I intend to deal with the matter as it affects the fishing industry in British Columbia and particularly in the Fraser river area. My purpose in rising at this time is at least to show where I stand on the question, and I trust that a solution may be 51952-36
found so that, if at all possible, a stop may be put to the entry of these people, and they may be placed on the same footing as those from other oriental countries.

maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no doubt it will be found that the members from British Columbia are unanimously in favour of the principle of the bill which has been introduced by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). I think the previous speakers are to be complimented upon the restraint they have exercised, because much might have been said that would have added to the bitterness and the racial prejudice which are becoming more and more evident in that province.
The chief arguments in support of the bill have been ably stated already. I merely wish to indicate my support of the principle incorporated in this measure, and to touch upon one or two phases of the problem as they appeal to me. I think there is no longer any point in encouraging immigration from Japan, particularly that class of immigrants that enters into direct competition with the workers in our industrial enterprises in British Columbia. Any further immigration can only serve to aggravate a problem of which all the representatives from British Columbia are fully aware and which in some respects casts a shadow over community development, harmony and cooperation in many areas in that province.
One point I wish to stress at this moment is that the situation is bringing about dangerous friction and racial prejudice, producing a tension in community life that is not to be desired. In my opinion this tension is due very largely to the growing distrust of the policy of the Japanese authorities with regard to this problem of immigration. There is a growing conviction-and no doubt on this score the government has definite evidence- that the agreement has been violated in many respects, to the disadvantage of the people of British Columbia. Whether or not that conviction or belief is well founded, the uncertainty exists, as the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has stated, because of the ambiguous terms of the gentleman's agreement. No one can be at all definite as to the number of people, particularly Japanese labourers, who are being admitted into the province at this time, and therefore I wish to indicate my support of the principle contained in this bill. I think there would be no better time to raise the barriers against immigration from Japan.
I had hoped that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni in his remarks would indicate just how he would suggest negotiations might

Japanese Immigration

proceed so that the barriers might be raised without precipitating any international complication. No doubt by proclaiming this amending bill at the proper time any such complication might be successfully avoided; but after some study of this problem I am definitely of the opinion that, in the interests of our own population in British Columbia, at this time we should not give the Japanese people any preferential consideration in regard to immigration regulations, and that in order to prevent any aggravation of a serious problem we should take definite steps to r'aise the bars against further immigration.

maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the bill before the house, and to congratulate the mover and also the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) upon the very able manner in which they have placed before the house arguments in favour of the measure.
I do not intend to go into details. All I wish to say is that for several years the matter has been brought before the house, and it has always been looked upon by the people of eastern Canada as one confined to British Columbia. But I think, now that trouble in the orient has developed, and in view of the rush on the part of the Minister of Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) to see that defences are built on the Pacific coast, that not only the government but the people in eastern Canada feel that the oriental problem in British Columbia is a Canadian problem.
I am not going into further particulars, but I would ask every hon. member, whether from Ontario, Quebec or the maritime provinces to take the measure into serious consideration. It has been said that we are a little late in closing the gate. I agree with that. It should have been closed at the time we closed the gate against the Chinese. There was just as much reason to close it against the Japanese. Due to that action there has been little or no immigration from China, and yet we are on the very best terms with that country.
I trust that the government may accept the bill and that it may become law, so that we may now close the gates and relieve the problem w'hich we have on the Pacific coast...
Mr. T. J. O'NEILL (Kamloops): Mr. Speaker, I would be remiss in my duty if I did not rise in support of the bill so ably presented by the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill). At the same time I should1 like to compliment him upon the able manner in which he presented the position of

British Columbia and, I believe, the position of Canada, with regard to the problem of oriental immigration.
May I also congratulate the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) upon his very able contribution. I, too, with the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil) am pleased at the lack of bitterness which has been shown by hon. members who have discussed the measure. Only those people who come from British Columbia can realize just what oriental immigration to that province really meatis. I was pleased to hear that the hon. member for Vancouver South is a native son of British Columbia. But, even at that, I think I have been watching the oriental problem in that province longer than he has. and probably I appreciate the problem as well as he does, even if he does come from Vancouver, where the great majority of Japanese are.
The oriental question in my constituency has reached the same proportions, in relation to the population, as it has in Vancouver. For instance, the tomato canning industry around Kamloops is almost entirely in the hands of Japanese, Chinese and Hindoos. To some extent the native Indians work when the tomatoes are being picked. Most of that business is in the hands of the Japanese.
Very little could be added to what has already been said. There are one or two observations, however, upon which I might spend a few moments. One of these is the difficulty the law enforcement officers of British Columbia encounter in making the orientals live up to the minimum wage laws. I believe the Japanese are the greatest offenders in this respect. Possibly their business methods are responsible for this fact. It may be that not any more than other people have they a desire to evade the law, but there is an evasion of the law by reason of their business method. For instance, there may be twenty employees in a shingle bolt camp who must operate under the minimum wage laws as laid down by the province. The Japanese evade the law by forming partnerships, and each man working in their shingle bolt camps would be working as a partner of the concern. They are all bosses, and the law would not apply to them. They will work for fourteen or sixteen hours, or as many daylight hours as there may be in a day, for half the wages a white man would receive for eight hour's work. I believe nothing more need be said, except to point out how utterly impossible it is for white labour to compete under those circumstances.
The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) has called attention to the illegal

Japanese Immigration
entry of Japanese. This may have been going on along the coast of British Columbia, from the northern end of Vancouver island up to Alaska, to a far greater extent than the Royal Canadian Mounted Police realize. By people who live in the country around there I am reliably informed that there come in many Japanese in what are supposed to be boats that are fishing in those waters. They are landed, and the boat goes back to Japan. I do not live in that part of the country and do not know whether this assumption is based on fact, but I have received reliable information to the effect that it is so.
I think the time has long since passed when we should have closed the door. But let us not wait until the white people have been forced to leave-because, either that must happen, or we must reduce our standard of living to that of the Japanese-I say we should close the door.
For these reasons I most heartily endorse the principle of the measure the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has introduced.

maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, probably it is not necessary to add much to what has been said in support of the measure. Perhaps it is desirable that we should not go much farther in the matter at this time. We do not know yet what action the government proposes to take with regard to the bill. But it should always be remembered-I think it has always been noted in the house-that hon. members from British Columbia have been a sort of listening post for the rest of Canada on this oriental question.
If hon. members would care to take the trouble to look back through -the volumes of Hansard they would find that the burden of the debates which have taken place in years past has to a great extent been borne by members from British Columbia. This is but natural, for it is in that province almost entirely that the question is driven home, time and time again, as to whether the time has come-indeed, if it has not passed-when Canada should say who should enter her ports of entry.
We must remember the delegation of four young Japanese who, two years ago, appeared before the special committee on the elections act, and I well remember the impression those four young people made on members of the committee other than those from British Columbia. I remember also how it was the duty of certain British Columbia members of that committee to draw to its attention certain facts on the opposite side of this question, and I need hardly say that the 51952-364
members from other parts of Canada were very much enlightened when they heard of what had been happening, the situation that had been growing up in British Columbia for the past generation. During the existence in the early days of this century of the Anglo-Japanese agreement, come to by the British government, I think, in the middle nineties, Canada's position was nothing like so clear as it has been since the amendment of that agreement. I do not know whether the Canadian government of that day was consulted by the British government or not, but Canada did find her hands to an extent tied by the existence of that agreement. That agreement was modified; Canada's hands were untied, and in my opinion for several years past it has been open for Canada to say to whom we should open our ports of entry.
Reference has been made to the fact that perhaps at the basis of this whole matter is the question of assimilability, and I think the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) is greatly to be commended for the delicate way in which he handled his reference to assimilability. We do not want on this occasion, or on any occasion, to speak words in the house which could in any way be taken as an affront by another country, one with whom we have been on friendly terms, one from whom we desire to buy and to whom we desire to sell those commodities which are mutually beneficial to both countries. We desire, therefore, to handle this matter as best it may be handled, remembering at the same time that we owe a debt not only to the people who were instrumental in placing us individually in this house but to all the citizens of Canada, and most particularly that we owe a debt to those who are not yet born in this country.

maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say just a very few words in connection with this matter. As has been already pointed out by members from British Columbia, the matter of oriental immigration into that province not only is one of considerable importance to British Columbia but eventually will be of importance to the whole of this dominion. The oriental problem has given me much concern over quite a number of years because it has never been faced honestly and squarely in this dominion. It has been made a political football on every possible occasion. The hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Barber) says that it is a little too late to close the gate. The gate should never have been opened. Greed for cheap labour brought the oriental to British Columbia, and greed for trade has kept him coming in.
Japanese Immigration

While I am in agreement with the bill brought before the house by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), I must say that the circumstances in which the bill is now brought before us are no better than they were two years ago when I raised the question here, and when my motion was unanimously voted down by both the major parties in the house. It is not often that one is vindicated so soon. On that occasion the hon. member for Comox-Alberni accused me of dishonesty in bringing the matter forward. Let me read his closing words in speaking to my resolution at that time. They will be found at page 387 of Hansard of February 20, 1936:
We have to take into consideration international and world-wide conditions to which the Prime Minister referred, and for that reason I acquiesced in the reduced immigration which, I say, is a great improvement on the open door policy arising from the gentleman's agreement which existed previously, and under which as many as 1,700 in one year came in. Although I know it would be popular in British Columbia that we upset the present agreement, I am not asking that we do so. I would ask that it be rigidly adhered to and enforced and, for the reasons stated, not enlarged. I earnestly hope the house will turn down the resolution.
