maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what I shall say about this question will be said in a very few words. If we will not grant the fullest rights of citizenship to a people, we should not permit them to root themselves in our land among our people and in our economic living. If these people will not or cannot assimilate with our Canadian people, then by that very fact they cannot be permitted peacefully or otherwise to take from us that which is ours.
We citizens of Canada should be permitted to avow allegiance to only one country, and no individual in Canada should be permitted to be and act as a Canadian who avows allegiance to more than one nation. He must forsake the one and cleave to the other, and be definite in that to which he allies himself. If gentleman's agreements are made-and, Mr. Speaker, there are such human beings as gentlemen-then, being made by gentlemen, those agreements should be kept. If the agreements are broken it appears that they were not made entirely by gentlemen, and if there is anything wrong with any agreement which permits an introduction of Japanese into our country, that agreement should be changed. So I feel that I must definitely support the bill sponsored by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), although I question that the government can do more than take the attitude of the house under counsel and advisement.
Japan is a feudal country, amazingly enj lightened by the industrial progress created in the British Isles in the nineteenth century, and sealed to every other country in the world. Bushido, the spirit of Japan, is a feudal spirit, and we cannot deal with the Japanese as we deal with our own people. Great men and great women there are among them, with amazing minds and fine intellects; but the measuring rod for us in our Canadian citizenship and all that it implies must definitely be applied to them, and if we cannot determine their acceptability by that measuring rod we must not allow them to use the Japanese rod on our Canadian backs.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext:
In view of the fact that the leader of the government may desire to make some observations on the question of policy, I think it desirable that I should present at this moment such remarks as I desire to make. First of all, I congratulate the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) upon the instructive speech that he made in proposing the second reading of this measure. I think that no member of the chamber can do otherwise than realize that

Japanese Immigration
the whole situation has been very thoroughly and carefully canvassed and that all the relevant features of what has taken place have been clearly placed before the house. I think it well also that the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green), who has very strong views on the subject, has dealt with the situation with great moderation.
I well recall when I first had the oriental question, so-called, brought to my attention. It is now between thirty-five and forty years since that took place. I was then engaged professionally in business that took me frequently to the coast, and one of the members of a provincial government, who subsequently sat in this house and is now in the senate- the uncle of the hon. member for Vancouver South-directed my attention to what he conceived to be the serious situation which would arise in Canada if the immigration of orientals continued and their numbers increased as rapidly as promised. I am frank in saying that it did seem to me to be ridiculous to think that a few hundred people might thus embarrass the national life of Canada.
A few years later I took the trouble to investigate what was taking place in a particular school area in the city of Vancouver. I also had occasion during the last ten years to make a fairly close study of what was occurring on the Pacific coast, in shipping and other activities of a certain portion of our oriental population, and I realized then that the hon. gentleman who spoke to me so many years ago was absolutely correct in his diagnosis. As regards the information that has been given to the house this afternoon and evening, dealing with the question of numbers, the method by which they came to our country, and their increase, these are all matters which I am sure the house has received with very serious concern, because, as it now appears, they are matters of tremendous importance.
I could add something to that; but in view of the fact that very special conditions prevail at the moment in China and Japan, it is not desirable that 'anything should be said in this Chamber which would give cause for acrimonious references or for either party to the conflict to believe that we were taking a position which was actuated by prejudice. It is quite clear, however, that in British Columbia a very serious situation is arising, and it may manifest itself in strange ways, unless we are exceedingly careful, within the next few months. The men with whom I have come in contact in recent weeks and months lead me to believe that their patience
is well-nigh exhausted. I appeal to some of my friends opposite if that is not a fair and correct statement of the situation.

maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext:
I would not for a moment have it thought that I desire to exaggerate by a hairbreadth so serious a matter, but I think I have not stated it too strongly in the terms which I have used.
That being so, I realize of course the difficulties of the government in dealing with the matter. I realize the difficulties, for instance, that I would have if I were called upon to deal with a situation that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has to deal with at this moment. Why? Because we are endeavouring to maintain, shall I say a measure of neutrality in a great conflict that has aroused the passions and prejudices of many people in many parts of the world. This is certainly not the time nor is it the place to discuss What I conceive to be the well settled national policy of the empire of Japan.
I quite agree with what was said this evening by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, that China must one day "come back." I care not who you are; if you have taken the trouble bo read something of the history of Chinese civilization; if you have read the Life of General Gordon as it applied to his experience in China, you cannot but realize that they are a very great people, a people numbering four hundred millions, Whose ancestors, a warlike race, swept over the whole of the country south of Manchuria and conquered wherever they went. These people, four hundred millions in number, will come back. At the moment they are, although not mortally stricken, engaged in a desperate conflict with one of the most highly mechanized and powerful nations in the world.
I repeat that it would be out of place to discuss what I conceive to be the national ambition of the Japanese empire. They have made it known to us at miany times and in definite terms; they have not been hesitant in expressing their views of what they believed their mission was, and their destiny, and they have indicated clearly on more than one occasion what they believe to be their place in Asia.
This is not the time to discuss the matter, but one may point out that this great dominion of ours marches upon the Pacific ocean. Our coastline on the Pacific is long; it is all in the province of British Columbia. Although I had intended to refer to the matter, I think perhaps I should not make any reference to what my investigations, such as
Japanese Immigration

they are, lead me to conclude to be the facts as to the knowledge that these people possess of our coastline, our ports, our harbours and our resources in British Columbia. I shall refrain from making that reference.
Now, as the government has endeavoured to maintain neutrality, my friend the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) has pointed out that our hands were tied in days gone by; for the action of the British government -I believe it was in the days of Lord Lans-downe at the Foreign Office-did not leave us that measure of freedom of action which we now possess and which we have possessed for some years. As we now possess that freedom of action and that ability to deal with the situation in its entirety, that ability which an autonomous people should possess, I think in our effort to maintain neutrality we should be fair to both the Chinese and the Japanese; and as we have placed absolute restrictions upon the Chinese, apart from the limited exceptions which have been referred to to-dav, and which really are no exceptions to the general prohibition, I think we should take similar action with respect to the Japanese.
I am wholly in accord with this measure; I do not believe that we should play favourites in this matter. On the other hand, an immediate action of that kind could only be construed in one way, having regard to the unfortunate conditions which prevail in the orient, and therefore I say to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni that as a member of this house, with a certain measure of responsibility and knowing something of the great burden of obligation that rests upon a government at a time like this in endeavouring to observe neutrality, I could not vote for a measure which did not restrict the operation of the act until such time as it came into force by proclamation. In any event I believe it would be. necessary to provide that the act should not come into force until proclaimed. It well might be that for reasons which are apparent it would be desirable, perhaps, rather than have the act come into force by proclamation, to fix a date a year hence, say, or whatever time might be regarded as reasonable, in order to enable the government to make such adjustments as might be decided upon through representations to the Japanese government and through negotiations carried on through diplomatic channels.
But, that action should be taken, I am bound to say to the right hon. the Prime

Minister I have no doubt. I say that with some hesitancy, because, when the matter was first brought to my attention some thirty-five years ago. I was of the view that a great people such as this nation, living in a vast area such as Canada, need have no concern about a few hundred people from the orient. I have stated already that I have had to change my opinion in the light of what has occurred. Indeed, I care not who you are; you cannot visit the Pacific coast of Canada; you cannot go up that coast as I have done in a boat and see the fishing operations, coming in contact and talking with those who have settled in our country and have attended our schools, without arriving at a definite conclusion. I suggest to the government, with a full realization of their difficulties and responsibilities, that we should not hesitate to declare ourselves as determined to maintain the same measure of treatment, now that we are free to do so, to those who come to our land from Japan as to those who come from China. This will make for peace; it will make for a better understanding, and in the end it will make for the development of our Canadian civilization. I am satisfied that that is so.
I think it would be unwise, Mr. Speaker, for one to say what crowds in upon one's mind with respect to this matter. I am not unmindful of exactly what is involved, and I shall content myself therefore with saying that with the principle of this measure I am wholly in accord. It is necessary if we are to maintain our neutrality between the great ancient empire of China, now in so sad a situation, and the young and vigorous empire of Japan-young in its present manifestations. If we are to maintain that measure of neutrality which the government is anxious to preserve, and if we are to assist in bringing about lasting peace by the action we take, I cannot but think that we must treat both the Chinese and the Japanese on exactly the same terms. If I remember my history, the more ancient civilization is that of China. It has behind it a record of achievement in arms, in arts, and in culture that leaves most of our western civilization somewhat envious. I believe that we must do what I have suggested if we are to maintain an even balance, a neutrality between those two countries.
On the other hand, not for a moment would I pass the bill in its present form. Without placing a time limit as to when it should come into force, or providing that it should become effective by proclamation, I think we would be courting a very serious situation indeed, and one which we could not contemplate at this particular moment, having

Japanese Immigration
regard to our earnest desire to keep our own country out of the conflict in Asia. I entreat the government to realize how serious the situation is, and I think I can say to the Prime Minister that his Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) has a clear appreciation of it. Having come into this country from the old land, without any inherited prejudices or any feeling of animosity in the matter, he has seen conditions as they have developed under his very eyes; his conclusions, I have no doubt, have been communicated to the Prime Minister in council and otherwise, and I believe that if his views are as unchangeable in tnis regard as they are upon the monetary problem, he will still feel, as he has expressed himself in times past, wholly in accord with the views which have been put forward this evening.
I repeat, however, that I would not for a moment suggest to the Prime Minister that the government should permit the bill to be enacted and go into force just as it stands, as a peremptory prohibition, without some provision which would enable the government for a year at least, through diplomatic channels and otherwise, to convey to the people of Japan the will of the parliament of Canada, that the gentleman's agreement, so-called, could no longer be made effective. If I were to say what was in my mind with respect to the gentleman's agreement, I think I would but read the report of the League of Nations and the Lytton report as indicating just why I would no longer call it a gentleman's agreement. I do not think I am going too far when I make that observation, though I shall not go further lest it be said that one has stirred up acrimonious feelings in a matter of this kind. I believe, however, now that we are free, as compared with our position in days gone by, to deal with this matter, that we should not hesitate to do so, because it is obvious that to permit a foreign power to determine who should come into this country under the terms of an alleged gentleman's agreement is a violation of all the rules which govern the national life of a country that pretends to be a nation, and is at variance with what I conceive to be the Japanese notion of a. self-respecting and independent thinking people, namely the Canadian people. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I have indicated the trend of my own thought and the conclusion my own observation has led me to with respect to this matter. I have endeavoured to make it clear to my fellow members that I conceive it to be a matter no longer concerning British Columbia only, but one which touches the life and hope and ambition and ideals of the whole Canadian people, and that the
longer action upon it is delayed the more difficult its ultimate solution is going to become.
One of the reasons why one hesitates to press for an immediate solution is to be found in the fact that events taking place in Asia would render it open possibly-possibly I say-to a wrong construction, and might place us in an invidious position in the eyes of the peoples of the world in our alleged endeavour to maintain neutrality. Therefore, while I should like to commend the hon. member who introduced the measure to the house, and hope that the government are prepared to accept the principle of it, I am one of those who, accepting that measure and believing strongly in it, would not for a moment urge its passing in its present form, as I believe it would be a very dangerous thing for us to do at this time. But I believe that we should pass it and add to it a section by which it would be provided that the measure should become effective only-I should think we might well say-on the first day of July, 1939. The hon. member for Comox-Albemi may think I am taking a great liberty with him when I make that suggestion, but I think the reasons for it will occur to him at once. 1 trust that in order that the whole Canadian people may be a unit in dealing with this question we may place ourselves on record in the manner indicated, and not embarrass the government in their endeavours to maintain neutrality by providing a lengthy period of time within which our friends-our friends I say-the people of Japan, may understand that the end of our patience has been reached and that we no longer desire to maintain an agreement which is predicated upon false principles and in its application has been found to be an incentive-I shall not use the strong word I should like to use-to entry into this country of large numbers of their citizens.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext:
I should like, Mr. Speaker, my first word on this measure to be one of thanks to the hon. members of the house who have participated in the debate for the moderation of tone which they have shown throughout in discussing a question which they recognize is of much wider concern than to our own country alone. I should like particularly to thank the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) for having helped to interpret to the house the position of the government in dealing with this situation at this time. I say frankly that I know of no single measure which has appeared on the order paper thus far, or of anything that is likely to come up for discussion in this parlia-
Japanese Immigration

ment, that has caused my colleagues and myself personally the same great concern as has the appearance at this particular time of the measure introduced by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). He himself has made quite clear in the debate this afternoon that the measure which he has presented is one of Japanese exclusion. I wish to emphasize that fact. The bill which we have before us at the present time, innocent as it may appear in its phraseology, and limited in its scope as the hon. member who introduced it has said it is, is nevertheless, according to his own statement, one of Japanese exclusion. That raises a question which is serious indeed. I would ask the house to consider whether in the light of the situation as we know it to-day, not only in the orient but throughout the world, it is advisable for this parliament at this time to enact an exclusion act against the Japanese.
The hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) in the course of his remarks said that he thought we should speak no words that can be taken as an affront to another country. With that sentiment I think we are all most heartily in accord. I think the house and the country are to be congratulated upon the fact that in the debate which has taken place today, in which hon. members have had perfect freedom to express their views, there has not been, unless one might wish to be censorious, a word spoken that could be taken as an affront by any nation. That is a very great relief to my own mind, knowing the responsibility which rests upon a government as to what may be said or done with respect to the different measures that come before the house. I remember in the debate on the address expressing the hope that hon. members would realize how very grave the international situation is to-day, and that things would not be said in this house which, however well they might be understood here, might be capable of being wrongly interpreted elsewhere, and that above everything we should be most :areful at this time to avoid adding any fuel o the flames of international strife which are iready far too widespread throughout the world. It is in questions of this kind that racial hatreds and prejudice have their roots. They serve so often to start a train of discussion that arouses or fosters international bitterness and hatred which lead in directions and to consequences of which those who may be responsible for them at the beginning have no conception whatever. So, to-day, in considering the position the government should take on this measure, up until almost the last moment I asked myself whether it 
would not perhaps be in the interests of Canada

and when I speak of the interests of Canada in this matter let me say I am thinking of the interests of the entire British Empire and of the democracies of the world at the present time-whether it would not be perhaps in the interest of us all that I should immediately follow the hon. member for Comox-Alberni and point out frankly to the house how a measure that meant Japanese exclusion if proceeded with at this time might be viewed on the morrow in Japan and by countries associated with Japan, and ask the house to allow me to move the adjournment of the debate. But the more I considered it the more I felt certain that hon. members would have a full consciousness of the seriousness of the international situation and could be expected to do just what they have done, namely, speak their minds quite frankly with respect to the problem, treating it as a national problem, which it is, but being careful in the expression of their views not to say anything which might foe capable of being misunderstood elsewhere.
I agree entirely that this is not a problem of British Columbia alone. Those of us who come from the other provinces of Canada must have an intense sympathy with the citizens of British Columbia who have had to carry pretty much the whole burden of one of the greatest national problems with which our country is faced. It is a grave and acute problem, and is presented in its gravest and most acute form in British Columbia. I would say to our friends from British Columbia that I am sure hon. members from all parts of Canada realize that they have a very grave situation to meet there, and that we all are most anxious to join with them in every possible way in furthering its solution. But we believe that they, as well as those of us from other provinces, will recognize that we have to be more than circumspect at this time as to the manner in which we seek to arrive at a solution.
My right hon. friend has spoken about his first interest in the question of oriental immigration, and referred to it as having been some forty years ago. I have on my desk at the moment a report on immigration to Canada from the orient and immigration from India in particular which, as Deputy Minister of Labour, I prepared for the government of Canada in 1908. My interest in the oriental immigration question arose naturally and inevitably in connection with the position which I held as Deputy Minister of Labour from 1900 until 1908, and also during the years

Japanese Immigration
immediately following when I was Minister of Labour. In the course of those inquiries I had the exceptional opportunity while visiting Great Britain of conferring with many of those who had most to do with oriental problems, and particularly problems of emigration as they affected India. Later I was sent on a mission to confer with the government of India on the question of emigration from India to Canada. Subsequently I went to both China and Japan to discuss with the governments of those countries matters affecting emigration from those lands to Canada. From that time to the present I have followed this question as carefully and as closely, I think, as any question that has interested me in public life. I have realized, as everyone must who looks at world trends and movements to-day, that despite what any government may do, each year makes more inevitable the drawing nigh of the day when we shall see how the great question of differences between the peoples of the orient and those of the Occident are to be finally settled, whether it is going to be possible to settle these differences by peaceful means, or whether we are to have in the end more in the way of international conflict as the only means of settlement.
I personally believe that everything which can be done that may avoid conflict, should be done. I think in the attempted solution of these great international problems, we should do everything we can to avoid the possibility of conflict, and it is from that point of view that the government takes its position with regard to this particular measure.
The hon. member for Comox-Albemi, as I have said, stated that the bill he had introduced was one providing for Japanese exclusion. He put it on the ground that we had excluded the Chinese and that therefore we ought also to exclude the Japanese. May I say that I agree with the view expressed by the right hon. leader of the opposition, which I think is the view of the hon. member for Comox-Albemi and, I might say, of all hon. members here, that so far as China and Japan are concerned, the citizens of those countries deserve like treatment in matters of this kind. I do not think there is any reason why the one people should be favoured more than the other. Indeed I would go further and say this, that all that bears upon the question of immigration from Japan or China also bears upon the question of immigration from India to Canada, with this in addition, that the problem as respects immigration from India is complicated still further by the fact that the natives of India are British subjects. So, in
considering this question, we must view it in the light of its bearings upon all the oriental peoples.
My belief is that the question of oriental immigration is best settled by agreement, if it can possibly be settled in that way, rather than by exclusion acts, which are offensive in the eyes of oriental peoples. There is no single measure, I think, more likely to arouse the indignation of a people than that an act, which is avowedly an exclusion act, should be enacted against them by another country. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni says, " Well, the Chinese do not take any exception to this. They seem to be quite satisfied." May I say to my hon. friend that he is entirely wrong in that assumption. The Chinese government and the Chinese people have resented very much the fact that they are totally excluded from Canada, and they have made representations to the government time and again to that effect. I remember that the former Chinese consul general in this city-notwithstanding a consul general has not the rank of a minister and therefore has not the same immediate approach to a government to speak in the name of his nation-when we were previously in office, repeatedly came and spoke about the wrong that China felt was being done her because of the act that had been passed by this parliament. When I was at the League of Nations in 1936, Mr. Wellington Koo, who has been the chief exponent of China in the trying times with which that country is faced at the moment, spoke to me very strongly about the harm that he thought our legislation was doing Canada in the eyes of the Chinese. He pointed out that he thought China might be one of the best markets for Canadian wheat; he thought China might be a good market for much of our other produce; that China had many reasons to have kindly feelings towards the dominion, but that to his certain knowledge the act we had passed had been to the prejudice of our trade with that country.

maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext: Was not the fundamental reason for their objection the discrimination that we exercise in allowing Japanese into the country and not allowing Chinese to come in?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext:
No, that was not it. I am glad my hon. friend has asked the question, for while that was mentioned, it was not the principal reason.
The question arises immediately as to whether the way to remedy a situation, if you have done an injustice in one direction, is to seek to perpetuate that injustice still further by similar action in another direction. I am
Japanese Immigration

not saying that we have done an injustice; I am simply stating the view which the Chinese government take of the situation, in having their nationals excluded from this country. I am not at all sure that an agreement might not be reached with both China and Japan on a reciprocal basis which would lead practically to no emigration at all from those countries to Canada or from ours to China or Japan. I do not think there are many people in Canada who in the yeans to come will wish to go as labourers or domestics either to China or Japan. I am sure, however, there will be many Who will wish to go as merchants, and others who would wish to go for purposes of trade. I believe the people of the orient are just as wise as we are in realizing that there is a great economic question here Which is bound to occasion perpetual misunderstanding between countries unless it is adjusted in some reasonable way, and I feel that if approached in the right manner they will be prepared to meet other countries in a spirit which will help to save the situation.
The problem is not one of inferior or superior races. It is not a racial problem at all. The problem is one of different civilizations, of different economic structures in the different countries. As long as there are those differences there is bound to be unrest as a consequence of immigration which leads to unfair and undue competition on the part of those who have lower standards of living and who may not assume the same measure of responsibility with regard to their citizenship as do the citizens of the country to which they come. I think it is from that broad point of view, that this question must be faced.
I do not agree with the statement that what is known as a gentleman's agreement cannot be kept. I shall give to the house figures which prove that in the last few years the gentleman's agreement between Canada and Japan has been kept. I venture to say that under no exclusion act would it be possible more effectively to restrict those coming into the country than has been the case under this arrangement, as administered *n the last few years, ever since, in fact, the opening of our legation in Japan.
Regardless of what legislation or agreement exists, undoubtedly there will always be efforts to smuggle men into other countries. That effort would go on under an exclusion act just as much as it would under a gentleman's agreement fixing numbers at a very few.

maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext: There is more difficulty about identification.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext:
No, no difficulty about identification, either, due to the way in which the existing agreement is being carried out. I shall have a word to say about that in a minute.
I am now pointing out that an agreement, supported by effective regulations, is just as capable of efficient enforcement as is any exclusion act. The experience of the last few years has taught us that conclusively.
I should like to say a further word about the Chinese attitude toward the present legislation. May I tell the hon. member for Comox-Alberni what has occurred since the beginning of this very year. When the new Chinese Consul-General, Doctor Chang-Lok Chen, who has just come to Canada, arrived in Ottawa, he came to call on me at my office, shortly after his arrival. Like many of his fellow citizens, Doctor Chang-Lok Chen is an exceptionally well informed and cultured gentleman. He is a graduate of the University of Chicago and of Yale University and holds the degree of Doctor of Philosophy. He acted as Consul-General in Calcutta, was a Consul-General in the United States, and is now in our capital as a Consul-General of China in this country.
On his first call Doctor Chang-Lok Chen spoke about our legislation against China. He made no mention whatsoever as to its being discriminatory against China in comparison with Japan. Rather he spoke of the friendly relations which he would like to see further developed between China and Canada. What he actually said was that his government hoped that when the unfortunate conflict in the east was ended we might find it possible to do for China what we had already done for Japan, namely send a minister to China who would be in a position to meet the Chinese government in the discussion of matters of mutual interest to the two countries, and who could be of assistance in helping to further what he believed would be a very substantial trade between the two countries. He was explicit, however, in saying that this subject could not even be tentatively discussed at the present time, because he realized that so long as there was a conflict in the orient, such as is proceeding to-day, he could not ask the government to consider the advisability of taking the step he had indicated. He thought that would not be possible until the conflict was completely over.
I said the present agreement with Japan was one which had been effective in restricting immigration from Japan to Canada. Be-

Japanese Immigration
fore I conclude I shall read to the house the statement I made on June 28, 1928, with respect to the agreement reached at that time. I am not going into the history of what occurred during the past forty, thirty, twenty-five or twenty years to account for the thousands of Chinese and Japanese who came into the country during that period. All hon. members know the reason for the numbers. We recall that there were those who were seeking to develop the province of British Columbia and who believed the best way to do it was to bring labour from the orient, just as in the early days when the United States was being developed labourers were brought from Africa and from other countries to help develop the new territories and resources of that country.
To-day we are reaping the fruits of greed and avarice-if one wishes to use those terms to describe the desire of men to enrich themselves as rapidly as possible. That is only a consequence of the great law which rules the conduct of nations as well as that of individuals. The children pay for the sins of their fathers, and the extent to which we in Canada to-day are suffering from an excess in the numbers of orientals in our country is due to the fact that there was a period, not so long ago, when the country was prepared to believe that it was desirable to permit large numbers of a class of coolie labour to come into Canada to build our railways, work our mines and help develop other of our resources.
Since that period has passed, each government, as it has been in office, has sought to meet the situation as effectively as it could, in the light of the then existing conditions. There are many factors we are apt to lose sight of as the years go by. For example, in connection with this very matter of Japanese immigration, we do not think about what the Anglo-Japanese alliance meant some years ago, more particularly to other parts of the British Empire than to our own, nor what was then felt by the government of the day in Canada in recognition of a responsibility with respect to any step taken by Canada which might have ill effects in other parts of the British Commonwealth of Nations.
I wish to point out particularly that any action taken by Canada which would occasion resentment by any country in the orient would be resented, not merely as a step on Canada's part, but with the relationship of all its parts what they are, as something to be resented against the whole British commonwealth. In the light of the present world
situation we cannot, whatever we do here, afford to lose sight of our obligation to other parts of the British Empire.
In seeking to deal with this matter of Japanese immigration it has been felt by all governments in Canada hitherto that a settlement by agreement, if it could be effected, was preferable to a step which was certain to be strongly resented. In his observations the hon. member for Yale made a further reference which I believe is worth keeping in mind. He referred to the obligation felt by hon. members from British Columbia toward those who returned them to this chamber. He referred as well to the obligation which all of us owe to those who will follow after us. I should like to emphasize that. In the working out of great international problems, nations do not forget the actions taken by one generation when, in a subsequent generation, a time comes to remember those actions.
I believe that acts of good-will and good intent are remembered equally with those which have occasioned resentment. If we can preserve good-will with other countries, and at the same time effect a satisfactory solution of our problems, we are not only serving our own generation, but serving future generations, and doing so in a much better way than we would by any other course.
My statement in 1928 was the following-

It is to be
found in the debates of this house for June 8, 1928, page 3980:
I am pleased to he able to inform the house that following conferences with the Japanese government, in which the Canadian government made clear the difficulties created in western Canada by the economic competition of Japanese immigrants, the Japanese Minister for Foreign Affairs has informed us through the Consul-General of Japan at Ottawa, that the government of Japan does not contemplate that the total number of emigrants to Canada, including agricultural labourers and domestic servants, and wives and children of Japanese emigrants resident in Canada, will exceed a total of 150 annually. We have further been informed that steps will be taken to terminate the practice of sending for so-called "picture brides." The administrative measures directed to this end will go into force on September 1.
The Canadian government has indicated to the government of Japan that hereafter in the case of immigration from Japan, as from other countries, the Immigration Act and procedure, including the provisions for viseing of passports and pre-investigation of applications will be administered by Canadian officials.
That was the position in 1928. The question that is most important at the moment is:

I can say to the house that it has been more than lived up to; that instead of the government having had difficulty in restricting I he numbers to 150, the numbers have not by actual check and count reached 150 per annum since the agreement was made. Since we have had our legation in Japan, each passport has been visaed by our own officers and inspected by our own immigration officials as these nationals of Japan have arrived in Canada. Let me give the figures. The administrative arrangements under the agreement did not come fully into practice until April 1, 1930, though the substance of the agreement became effective from September 1>, 1928. It will thus be seen that the number of Japanese immigrants entering Canada has been well within the maximum provided in the agreement. Tor the eight years from 1929 to 1937 the average is practically 100 a year, and for the past five years the average number has fallen to 81 a year.
Now I ask hon. members of the house, What is to be gained by passing an exclusion act at this time when, under an agreement made with Japan, the government of this country is bound to admit, and is glad to admit, that during the past five years the total number of Japanese who have come in under that agreement has not averaged over 81 per annum ?

maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister a question?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext: Certainly.

maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext: How does the Prime Minister account for the discrepancy between the figures he has given and the figures shown in the report of the Department of Mines and Resources, at pages 242 and 243? The figures there are quite different and show that in three or four years the gentleman's agreement was not kept.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext:
I am glad the hon. gentleman has asked the question, because he is not distinguishing between Japanese nationals admissible under the agree-
ment, and Japanese who are admissible as British subjects. The figures he is looking at, if I am not mistaken, include not only those who have come in under the agreement but in addition some who have come in as of right, a right which they would have under an exclusion act, namely, as British subjects. They include Japanese British subjects who have been abroad and have come back to Canada, or have gone abroad and married and have brought their wives back to Canada, or have had a family and brought its members back to Canada. That is a right which every Canadian citizen has. When a man is a Canadian citizen he has the right, even if he does not take advantage of it, to have a wife and family and to bring them in from any country. It is in the exercise of that right that some of these Japanese have come back, thereby increasing the total. I was just going to give those additional figures to the house.

maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext: I think it was stated in the terms of the agreement which the right hon. the Prime Minister quoted a few minutes ago that the 150 would include the wives of Japanese who went from Canada as naturalized subjects, married abroad and brought their wives back.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext:
No, I did not make any reference to them. What I said was this:
The government of Japan does not contemplate that the total number of emigrants to Canada, including agricultural labourers and domestic servants, and wives and children of Japanese emigrants, resident in Canada, will exceed a total of 150 annually.

maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext: Surely that third classification covers just these cases-Canadian Japanese who went back to Japan.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext:
No. If a
Japanese comes to this country who is not already a citizen, and brings his wife with him, she in addition to himself is counted as one of the quota of 150. If he comes back with a wife and five children, six additional of the quota have been taken up: the wife and children, with himself, making seven in all. Counted in that way the total quota has not been reached, and the figures I have given are the correct ones.

maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext: Actually the immigrants who have come in for several years have exceeded the number of 150, have they not?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: APPLICATION OF PROVISIONS OF CHINESE IMMIGRATION ACT, REVISED STATUTES, 1927. CHAPTER 95
speechtext:
I am coming to just what the number was. Let me make it perfectly clear that the agreement relates to Japanese nationals coming to Canada, whether they be men, women or children, and

Japanese Immigration
the quota cannot exceed 150, and it has not exceeded 100 on the average in the years the agreement has been in force. The average for the last five years has been about eighty-one.
Of the other group, those who are British subjects, who have been back in Japan for a time and have returned to Canada and brought with them wives and children, there have been a certain number, but the addition is not anything like the hon. member for Comox-Albemi would have the house believe. I shall give the house the exact particulars.
There are a limited number of Canadian nationals of the Japanese race entering Canada each year. These are, of course, completely outside the agreement. For the most part they are wives or children of Canadian nationals who returned to Japan and married, and later have come back to Canada. The number in the past eight years averages twenty-five women and fewer than ten children a year. In the past five years only fourteen women and three children a year have come in.
The complete total of immigration from Japan is to be found in the figures I have given, and I say, Mr. Speaker, that if there are any others outside that number who have come in, they have come in surreptitiously and illegally, and they could and, in all probability, would come in in exactly the same way, though perhaps in larger numbers, if there was an exclusion act.
In the light of these figures, which cannot be challenged, for they are authentic, as recorded by our own government officials who have been watching the whole business very closely, I ask hon. members, Is it desirable at this time to go further and pass an act which will totally exclude the Japanese? What would be the effect of passing such an act? We have one instance of record which might help us to discover what would be the result. The United States Government in 1924 passed an act. They did not call it an exclusion act, but it came to that, and the minute that act was passed an international situation developed which was a very, very serious one indeed, one the like of which I think none of us would care to see precipitated at this particular time. Let me give the house the particulars because they illustrate exactly what would inevitably follow from the course which the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has suggested, were it adopted as his bill proposes.
The United States law of 1924 took the form of an amendment excluding "aliens ineligible to citizenship." Under existing statutes, citizenship of the United States was confined to persons bom in the United States, regardless of race, and to naturalized persons,
naturalization being limited to "free white persons and to aliens of African nativity and to persons of African descent." While aimed at the Japanese, it applied to all Asiatics. According to the Japan Chronicle, an English paper published in Kobe:
No diplomatic event for many years aroused so much comment and excitement as the passage of the exclusion law in the United States.
Resolutions of both houses of the Japanese diet, public demonstrations, newspaper articles, missionary societies, all protested vigorously.
If that was the case in 1924 upon the enactment of an act by a great country like the United States, I wonder what would be the effect in Japan to-morrow if it were announced that one of the British dominions-and it would not be distinguished at all from the British Empire as a whole-had taken this particular measure.
May I pause here to say that one of the most regrettable features of the international situation to-day is that there are busily at work in Japan at the present time numbers of persons who are doing all they possibly can to foment differences between Japan and Great Britain. That is generally known. The British government in its reports has referred over and over again to that fact. It has endeavoured to have the public distinguish between what is the true feeling and the feeling that is being stirred up for ends that are anything but justifiable or worthy. That is the situation to-day. We must remember also that in every country to-d'ay which is engaged in conflict there is a peace party as well as a war party. It so happens that in some countries the war party has gained control. That is the situation in Japan; and the party in control has taken measures with which, unquestionably, a large number of the people have no sympathy. There are those in Japan who are struggling to maintain the friendship which has existed over so many years between the British and the Japanese, and I say that we, as one of the dominions of the British commonwealth, ought to do, and I believe will do, all that we can to preserve that friendship to the greatest degree possible, and certainly we ought to do nothing to increase the emnity that is being fostered.
I have in my hand a copy of a treatise on Oriental Exclusion, by Mr. R. D. McKenzie Ph. D., professor of sociology in the University of Washington. Let me read a paragraph or two of what is said in that publication about the effect upon the Japanese, and the Chinese of the United States act of 1924. At page 42 the writer says:
To the Chinese the act of 1924 was but another form of persecution and "gratuitous affront" added to a condition that was already severe enough.
Japanese Immigration

At page 45:
To the Japanese, the passing of the law came as a bolt from the blue, at once a suggestion of lack of national good faith in carrying out the gentlemen's agreement, and a reflection on national pride and racial dignity. The Japanese opposed the act during the period of its inception and still oppose it on political rather than on practical grounds.
Then he quotes what is an extremely interesting and valuable dispatch, one which bears directly on the measure that is before us at the present time. It serves to illustrate what we might expect if the bill of the hon. member from Comox-Alberni were to be enacted. It is a communication from Ambassador Hanihara to Secretary Hughes of the United States dated April 10, 1924. This is what the Japanese ambassador had to say to the government of the United States:
To Japan the question is not one of expediency but of principle. To her the mere fact that a few hundreds or thousands of her nationals will or will not be admitted to the dominions of other countries is immaterial, so long as no question of national susceptibilities is involved. The important question is whether Japan as a nation is or is not entitled to the proper respect and consideration of other nations. In other words, the Japanese government asks of the United States government simply that proper consideration ordinarily given by one nation to the self-respect of another, which after all forms the basis of amicable international intercourse throughout the civilized world.
In concluding his volume, this writer, at page ISO, makes the following observation after a careful study of the whole situation:
Exclusion differs from restriction principally in the mental attitudes involved. The practical results of the two methods are about the same. Each limits the number of arrivals. Each presents about the same kind of individual and administrative problems. Exclusion, however, differs radically from restriction from the standpoint of group attitudes. Exclusion discriminates in a manner that is offensive to the racial and national dignity of the group excluded. This is especially true when exclusion is based on the principle of ineligibility to citizenship. For then it conveys the obnoxious implication that the people excluded are biologically inferior.
Both China and Japan, according to the repeated utterances of their representative leaders, accept the principle of immigration restriction. They realize that it is in the interests of all concerned to prevent a too rapid intermingling of the races. They do object, however, to being discriminated against on the basis of race when such discrimination is unnecessary to achieve the end desired. There seems to be no fundamental difference of opinion regarding the objective. The conflict arises in connection with the method employed. It has been pointed out on numerous occasions

that the quota principle, as at present applied to Europeans, if applied to Asiatics, would admit such a negligible number that the practical end of exclusion would be achieved and without the sacrifice of international good-will.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that these are words of wisdom, which should be carefully pondered at this time with respect to the course that is proposed in this bill.
My right hon. friend the leader of the opposition has said that he agrees that the bill should not become operative immediately but that a date should be fixed some time hence when it would come into force. May I ask the right hon. gentleman if he really believes that this would at all relieve the situation which would be certain to develop once parliament passed a measure of this kind. I come back to what the hon. member for Yale said, that he hoped no words would be uttered in this house which would cause any affront to any nation. Well, if that is the hope of all of us here, must we not be doubly careful to see, not only that no words cause an affront but, what is much more important, that no act of the parliament of Canada causes an affront? That is the really serious thing. That is a consequence we have to consider with regard to this measure.
Other countries will understand that in our parliament as in all parliaments hon. members express themselves in different ways, some may say things which they themselves later on may come greatly to regret; and most countries fortunately are prepared to make allowances for that kind of thing. But when it comes to a parliament enacting a measure, there one nation speaks to another. I therefore submit that at this time, with the affairs of the world what they are, this parliament of Canada should not contemplate for one minute placing, an exclusion act upon its statutes, especially an act directed against Japan, where we have before us the evidence that, so far as Japan is concerned, she has been perfectly loyal to the agreement that now exists and has more than carried out its terms.
I know that at a time like the present, with feelings aroused as they have been by the conflict in the orient, passions are more easily stirred, people discuss these questions much more freely; they go much further in their language and assertions; reports become exaggerated, and little by little a new situation is created. And I am afraid it is only too true that in British Columbia at the present time there is an extremely serious situation arising from that very fact, and from the further fact that the depression has empha-

Copyright Amendment Act
sized the extent of the competition of the oriental with our own people. I would ask this question however:	Shall we be making
the situation any better so far as British Columbia is concerned if we take the course that is proposed here to-night? Would not the effect rather be, so far as British Columbia is concerned, that instead of being faced with one problem, which is very difficult, that province would be faced with a second problem which would be equally menacing if not more dangerous? We are finding it necessary now to take what steps we possibly can to ensure the security of the people of British Columbia. We must, therefore, be doubly careful to see that our actions give no cause for offence.
During the past few years and particularly of late the government has been investigating very carefully and fully the matter of surreptitious immigration into the country. As I have said, whether you have an exclusion act or you limit by agreement, there are bound to be efforts at entry on the part of those who wish to get into the country and who are not free to do so under existing arrangements. Those efforts may succeed in part; for although a country does its best in its administration of its laws, it is not possible entirely to frustrate such efforts. But the different departments of this government have been exercising a careful scrutiny of the whole situation, and in the light of recent developments, doing so to an extent that has not been attempted in the past. The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) mentioned this evening that he himself had learned that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police had discovered many cases of illegal entry and that some nine hundred persons had been sent out of the country in consequence. The officials of the immigration department, the fisheries department, the external affairs department, the mounted police, the intelligence branch of the defence department, have all been working together, at Ottawa, with respect to regulations, and in British Columbia in actually seeking to enforce the laws and regulations and to prevent aliens from coming into the country surreptitiously and to send out those who have come in illegally. They have been doing so of late to a degree that has never been attempted heretofore. We intend to intensify that investigation into illegal entries into Canada, and I wish to assure the house that everything that the government can possibly do to prevent anything in the nature of illegal entries will be done.
With that assurance, Mr. Speaker, perhaps I have said enough to cause the house to feel
that I would be justified in moving the adjournment of this debate. I think it would be unfortunate were hon. members compelled, with the international situation what it is to go on record at this particular time with regard to this bill. A division would certainly serve only to place in a very false position many of those who are desirous of doing only what is best from a national and international point of view and who realize that the time has come when we must look at all controversial questions in the light of the present world situation. Their position would certainly be misunderstood. There are, I know, many who for local reasons would wish to support the measure, who for international reasons might well feel they could not. I hope they may be spared that necessity.
I would therefore move that this debate be now adjourned, and in doing so I hope the house will fully appreciate the motives which actuate the government in taking that step.

maintopic: COPYRIGHT AMENDMENT ACT, 1931   FURNISHING OF LIST OF DRAMATICO-MUSICAL OR MUSICAL WORKS OWNED OR CONTROLLED- PUBLIC RADIO RECEPTION OR GRAMOPHONE REPRODUCTION

speechtext:
Mr. W. K. ESLING (Kootenay West) moved the second reading of Bill No. 12, to amend the Copyright Amendment Act, 1931.
He said: I desire to preface my remarks on this bill with the assurance to hon. members that it does not in any way prejudice the rights and privileges of authors or composers. It does not refer to literary copyrights; it refers only to dramatico-musical or musical works. Specifically the bill refers to the Canadian Performing Right Society, a corporation engaged in the business of acquiring copyrights and collecting fees in compensation for the use of music. This society claims to hold, by assignment, from the
Copyright Amendment Act

American society and from English and European societies the copyright to between two and three million titles, but in reality it does not know just what it does own. It claims to own practically everything on the air, and with that assumption there has been no interference. The society has actually registered between 150,000 and 200,000 titles and the purpose of the amendment to the Copyright Act is to require the society to furnish to those from whom it exacts payment a certified list of the music which it actually does control.
Invariably when an amendment to the Copyright Act is suggested we are reminded Canada is a signatory to the Berne international copyright convention and that as such we have certain obligations. May I again assure hon. members that this bill does not in any way violate any such obligation. Successive international conventions have made it clear that the means of redress and the extent of protection of authors and composers are governed exclusively by the laws of the country in which protection is sought. Canada has an excellent Copyright Act. It affords to composers and authors as much protection as is afforded by the copyright act of any country in the world.
The purpose of this amendment is to protect the public. This bill is not offered in a spirit of partisanship, because the Copyright Act has been administered by governments of both parties. The great difficulty is in the wording of one section, which gives this society authority to collect fees for all the music which it claims to own. Now that is a pretty large order, because a man can claim almost anything. Not many hon. members pay out money to someone merely because he claims a right to collect it; they want to know more about it. It is this authority claimed by this society which has permitted it to run wild. It has run so wild, has carried on its business by such aggressive apd dictatorial and oppressive measures that it has harassed the small users of music. Surely it cannot be said that the proposal merely to require this society to furnish people with a list of the music it controls is a very great burden. If a person in British Columbia, say Prince Rupert, desires to know from this society whether it has the copyright on a certain piece of music the society simply tells him to go to Ottawa and ascertain for himself. That is not a very courteous answer. Those people far away cannot, without considerable difficulty, send to Ottawa or have people in Ottawa look up for them a copyright registration. I have printed matter showing that

if you write to the society asking whether they control this, that or the other piece of music the society maintains the right to charge for the information.
As to the exact ownership of these two or three million titles which the society claims, let us see whence it comes. In the first place there was an assignment from the American society. The American society is not in very good odour in the United States. If hon. members were to look at the magazine Time, the issue of December, 1935, they would find that four very large companies owning about forty per cent of the music controlled by the American society had withdrawn from that society and they did not return to the fold for nearly a year. Yet the Canadian society is collecting fees from Canadian citizens for music belonging to a company which had withdrawn from the American society. Therefore it is not a very dependable assignment. Furthermore, if you look to the United States, you find that the American society is in continuous trouble; that the states of Washington, Montana, Nebraska, Wisconsin and Florida have outlawed the society by legislation, and that some eighteen other states have passed legislation to curb its activities. In Canada we find that twice the Manitoba legislature has passed resolutions asking this government to curb the activities of this society. It is because of the society's oppressive tactics and because of complaints which I have from my own district that I think it advisable to refer to some of them.
Take first the fact that this society is capitalized with ten thousand shares of which only two are held in this dominion, the remainder being owned in the United States and England. The society is practically dictated to by the directors in New York. The society started collection of fees at a minimum of $10. There never was a maximum limit. Then the charges increased in accordance with certain conditions and the number of times music was produced. Then arbitrarily the society raised the minimum fee to $30. It was that increase and the many protests which resulted from it which brought about the appointment of His Honour Judge Parker as a royal commissioner to inquire into the matter. What did he find? Hon. members will see from his report that there were no Canadian authors having membership in the society, no Canadian authors or composers participating in its profits; that the funds collected were remitted to the United States after deducting only sufficient to carry the overhead. It was as a result of that report that the government appointed this appeal board to revise the society's tariff.

Copyright Amendment Act
That appeal board is to be commended, because had they not acted as they did we do not know what figure these fees would have reached. First there was a minimum of $10; then up it went to $30, then down to $5, a figure fixed by the appeal board. And where the society went out to collect $30 and could not get $30 they were willing to take $20, and if they could not get $20 they would take $10. I know of specific instances in my own community.
They also take advantage of the fact that the government through the appeal board revises their tariffs. They say to the people: This is our tariff as revised and approved by the government appeal board. The application forms also refer to their repertoire. It is an application to use the society's repertoire and the licence issued is a permission to use the society's repertoire. Well the society has no repertoires and never had. It does not know to-day what it owns. When they tell us through their paid lobbyists who have been patrolling the corridors of this building that it would be impossible to prepare a list, that a list would be so expensive, I do not think it is asking very much, because a list of the works this society owns would hardly make a book larger than the Montreal telephone directory.
The provision is that titles shall bear the date of the copyright, so that it may be readily seen when that copyright expires. Then, as occasion requires, additional leaves can be handed the licence holders in order that they may know what is the new music. As to the work which they contend the preparation of these lists will entail, I should like members to read some of the application forms and the printed matter of this society, in which they impose upon licence holders requirements which are absolutely incredible. First of all they ask the applicant to fill out his forms according to periods. That period may be for a week, for a month or for a quarter, and when he makes that application he undertakes to fill out a weekly, monthly or quarterly report. Then they require him to tell, first of all, whether the music is vocal or instrumental or mechanical. They want him to tell whether it is produced by a piano, a piccolo, a gramophone, a saxophone or a radio. They want him to tell the name of the author and the name of the arranger and he must tell just how many minutes, how many hours and how many days this music is performed.
Then they tell the applicant how to arrive at the basis of charges, and I am reciting this because it indicates the work which this corporation imposes upon applicants from whom it seeks to collect licence fees. Why, it requires one to tell first of all the title of the 51952-37
music and how many minutes that music has been played. Then it says that a certain charge is made to hotels, to restaurants, even to boarding houses, to cabarets, to skating rinks, to stores and all down the line in these places where small music is performed and where it was never intended that licence fees should be collected. They say the charges against these various places of business are to be calculated on the hour performance basis. The hours of performance are calculated, first of all, by multiplying the number of musicians, the greatest number of musicians, including the leader and soloist, in any one performance in any one hour of the time by the number of hours. Then you carry on a series of calculations and multiplication. You multiply that by the greatest number of days on which music is produced. Then you multiply the greatest number of days by the greatest number of weeks in any period. Then you multiply that by the rate of one and a half cents an hour, as they put it, and you must make your report accordingly. On that basis is fixed the rate that one must pay. Then, worse than that, if you fail to make that report the printed matter of the society tells you that the fees which you have already paid will revert to the company, and if you continue to use this music without having dbtained another licence you are said to be infringing the Copyright Act.
At a previous session I referred to this society as a racket. Well, it has had that designation from many sources. I said that it carried on its business by way of threats. Well, the president of the society took exception to that and threatened a libel suit. I looked up the dictionary and found that the best or rather the most charitable interpretation of the word "racket" was "a system of securing money to which one is not entitled." I think that applies very well to this society when it attempts to Collect fees for music of which it is not the owner. I also cited the case of the Eaton Amateur Dramatic Society, which sought to put on the Pirates of Penzance, and obtained a quoted price from the broadcasting station. They were told that they would have to get a quotation from the Canadian Performing Right Society, and they obtained a rate of $61. The broadcasting station thought that was so excessive that they turned the matter over to their solicitor, who found that the Pirates of Penzance was no longer copyright but was in the public domain, and that this society had no right whatever to collect fees on that work. That is just one incident, and I do not think it unreasonable a,t all to ask this society to supply to those from whom it seeks to collect fees a list of the music for which it demands payment.
Copyright Amendment Act

Another amendment to this act is in connection with the small users of radio music and, as I say, it is a matter in which every constituency in Canada is interested, since it affects every hotel, every dining room, restaurant, skating rink, store, lodge hall and so on. It was never intended that these people should be penalized by the collection of these fees. The amendment to this act simply says that these small places shall not pay for music which they receive over the radio. The appeal board was given a tariff at the end of November, with a request from this society that the various broadcasting stations pay to it for the year 1938 the sum of $145,000. The appeal board cut that sum down to $83,000, which was a pretty good cut. It just indicates that this society is rather reckless in its charges. But that $83,000 applies only to receiving sets for domestic purposes, in other words receiving sets in homes. Of this $83,000, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation pays to this society the sum of $32,000. So the men having radios in these little places of business, having paid the government licence fee, feel it is not right that they should be called upon by this society to pay additional fees.
Those are the principal features of this bill, and I h'ope that hon. members will look upon it not as a party matter but simply as a means of serving their constituents by requiring this society to hand them a list of such music as they claim to control.

maintopic: COPYRIGHT AMENDMENT ACT, 1931   FURNISHING OF LIST OF DRAMATICO-MUSICAL OR MUSICAL WORKS OWNED OR CONTROLLED- PUBLIC RADIO RECEPTION OR GRAMOPHONE REPRODUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having noticed certain abuses arising from the interpretation of the Copyright Act in matters of radiobroadcasting, I wish to point out to the house some of them which will indicate, I believe, the importance of passing, if not the two proposed amendments, at least the second one, which relates to licences required of owners of receiving sets. It might have been better to change the definition of the word "performance" in paragraph 2 of the act. However, the amendment contained in paragraph two of the present bill will remedy many abuses, and I am glad to support it.
The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Esling) has already explained the methods of the Canadian Performing Right Society, which monopolizes copyrights and uses them not for the benefit of authors but for its own benefit and at the expense of the public. I shall merely point out the case of hotels, restaurants and clubs. In every village there is at least one hotel, restaurant and store which have one or more radio receiving sets used by the inmates or by visitors. The set is in operation the whole

day and even the entire evening, broadcasting the news of the day, sports news, hockey games, musical compositions, etc. Should there happen to be broadcast in the course of the day or evening a musical work or a song subject to copyright, the merchant, restaurant keeper or hotelkeeper whose receiving set was operating at that moment and who has not paid a copyright fee or obtained a licence becomes liable to an action in damages or a penalty of as much as $200, even although copyright fees had been paid by the station broadcasting the music or the song. Mark well, the hotelkeeper, merchant or restaurant keeper did not select the song or musical work, which indeed may annoy him; the choice is made by the broadcasting station. More than that, Mr. Chairman. Supposing that in the Royal Y'ork hotel in Toronto, for instance, the orchestra should broadcast a musical composition, the hotel has to pay a copyright or licence fee to the company holding the copyright. The station broadcasting the composition or song also has to pay a licence or copyright fee. And the small village hotelkeeper, merchant or restaurant owner who happened to leave his radio open during that time has likewise to pay a licence or copyright fee. Should he not do so he becomes liable to an action for damages or to a penalty of as much as $200.
A similar situation exists in the cities; in fact, I may say that it is even worse. Take the case of the Chateau Laurier in Ottawa. Should a musical work or a song be broadcast from there by a radio station, the hotel wrould have to pay a licence fee for having performed the composition; the station would have to pay a licence fee for broadcasting it, and the hotel would have to pay a third licence fee for any receiving set situated within its walls. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that that is pure exploitation and that it is time to put an end to it.
It is objected in certain quarters that the proposed act would constitute a contravention of the Berne international convention. The Berne international convention was concluded in 1886 and revised in Berlin in 1908. Surely this convention, signed in 1886 and revised in 1908, could have no relation to radiobroadcasting which at that time did not even exist. Broadcasting began in a practical way only in 1921 when the first licences were issued to stations in the United States. It has since developed in the different countries.
In 1927, at the second International Juridical Conference on wireless telegraphy held at Geneva, at which most of the countries of

Copyright Amendment Act
the civilized world were represented, there was submitted the following proposition: "Copyright fees are paj-able as well by all proprietors or operators of receiving sets in a public place." This proposition, Mr. Chairman, was rejected by seven votes against three, with three delegations not voting.
One year later, in 1928, at the conference convened in Rome for the purpose of revising the Berne Convention, the opinions were still uncompromising. And those who followed its proceedings declare " that it would not have been possible to attain an agreement if the question of public receiving sets had been discussed." Indeed, the Court of Amsterdam decided in 1929 that " according to the law of 1912, the word performance may be applied only to the fact of performing the work at the broadcasting station where such work will be broadcast."
On the 20th of January, 1930, the Court of Copenhagen delivered a similar decision. On the 19th of October, 1931, the High Court of Germany, although Germany like the other countries already mentioned, was a signatory to the Rome Convention of 1928, decided that:
The operating of a receiving set does not constitute a new process from the legal point of view, but only a part of a complex broadcasting process which begins with the production of sounds in front of the microphone of the broadcasting station, and ends with the reconstitution of the sounds by an indefinite number of receiving sets. And this complex whole represents a "public performance" or a "commercial reproduction" of the musical work.
If section 11 bis of the Rome convention, by which the word " broadcasting " was added, were to cover the case of receiving sets, the Court of Copenhagen, the Court of Amsterdam, and the High Court of Germany, all of countries signatory to the Berne and Rome conventions, surely could not have rendered such decisions.
So that, according to the interpretation of the conventions of Berne and Rome by the three nations I have just mentioned and who were signatories to those conventions, nothing stands in the way of the proposed legislation exempting radio receiving sets from copyright fees.

I might add the opinion of a jurist who is a specialist in the matter, 51052-37$
Hoffman, who stated at the fourth International Juridical Conference of 1930:
The person who installs a loud speaker is not giving a performance, he is simply divulging the performance of somebody else.
The same opinion is held in the United States. For instance, in a case decided in the State of California, where the broadcasting station had obtained permission to broadcast the author's protected works, Judge McCormick made the following statement:
The performance in such cases, takes place in the studio of the broadcasting station, and the operator of the receiving set in effect does nothing more than one would do who opened a window and permitted the strains of music of a passing band to come within the enclosure in which he was located. It is true that it is the voluntary act of the person turning the dial on the receiving set that enables electricity to animate the mechanism so as to make audible within hearing distance of the receiving set that which is disseminated from the broadcasting station, and which is on the air by reason of the broadcast, but such voluntary action, in my opinion, is far from "performing" the copyrighted work. The performance, which is licensed as just stated, occurs entirely in the studio of the broadcasting station, where the copyrighted musical composition is lawfully used, and the action occurring at the receiving set is simultaneous therewith, and is in no sense a reproduction of the musical composition that is being lawfully performed at the broadcasting studio. The action, play, and use of the copyrighted composition has been completed within the studio.
Mr. Speaker, I think it would be unfair to ask a fee for a radio receiving set from people who have no control whatever over programs selected by the broadcasting station. As a result of such a policy, any receiving set owner would have to khut his radio when speeches, addresses, the day's news, market quotations, musical programs are broadcasted lest he might happen to listen to some song coming from a broadcasting station and subject to copyrights held by the Canadian Performing Right Society.
That, I think, would be both arbitrary and abusive. The Canadian Performing Right Society is already collecting a royalty through the licence fee from the performing artist; it is also collecting a second royalty through the licence fee paid by the broadcasting station, and a third one for the same work from the owner of the receiving set. The simple mention of the fact is sufficient to prove the absurdity of such a proposition.
These facts, Mr. Speaker, and also the authorities I have just quoted tend to prove conclusively, to my mind, that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Kootenay-West does not interfere with the Berne convention as amended by the Rome convention; the effect of this amendment, if adopted
